fields.title: They Were Young – Book 2: Tested
fields.subtitle: Six whose faith was tried before they were grown
fields.description: Six true stories for readers aged 13 to 17 of people whose faith was tested while they were young: a British teenager kidnapped to Ireland; a Sudanese girl enslaved as a child who chose freedom before the Italian authorities; a young mother in Carthage who kept a prison diary; the pages of a Ugandan king who would not deny Christ; a rebellious sailor saved in a storm; and a Sikh boy who burned a Bible and then met Jesus. The second book of They Were Young.
fields.about_html:
They Were Young is an original Ochorus series of true stories for readers aged 13 to 17 about people whose faith began, or was tested, while they were young. Book 2, “Tested”, gathers six whose faith was tried by captivity, persecution, loss and their own rebellion.

Patrick was kidnapped from Britain at sixteen and learned to pray as a slave in Ireland, then went back to the people who had enslaved him. Josephine Bakhita was stolen from her home in Sudan as a child and later, before the Italian authorities, chose to stay free. Perpetua, a young mother in Carthage, kept a diary in prison before she was martyred in 203. The young pages of Kabaka Mwanga of Buganda refused to deny Christ and died at Namugongo in 1886. John Newton was forced into the navy at eighteen and cried out to God in a storm at twenty-two. Sundar Singh burned a Bible at fifteen and, days later, met Jesus.

The stories are true and told without graphic detail. Where a tradition is legend rather than history, they say so. Each ends with the person’s own words where we have them, four questions to think through, and a pointer to read on in the library. Book 1 is not required.

qa.question: What is Book 2 of They Were Young about?
qa.answer: Six true stories of people whose faith was tested while they were young: by kidnapping and slavery, by persecution and martyrdom, and by their own rebellion. Each chapter tells one life in full, lingering on the years when the test came.

qa.question: Who is in Book 2?
qa.answer: Patrick of Ireland, Josephine Bakhita, Perpetua of Carthage, the Uganda Martyrs, John Newton and Sadhu Sundar Singh: people from Britain, Sudan, North Africa, Uganda and India across sixteen centuries.

qa.question: Is it suitable for teenagers?
qa.answer: Yes. It is written for readers aged 13 to 17. It is honest about slavery, kidnapping and martyrdom but never graphic, and the hardest moments are told with care.

qa.question: Are the stories true?
qa.answer: Yes. They are drawn from the people’s own writings, such as Patrick’s Confession, Perpetua’s prison diary and Newton’s narrative, and from the earliest accounts. Later legends, such as Patrick and the snakes, are named as legends.

qa.question: Do I need to read Book 1 first?
qa.answer: No. Each book stands on its own. Book 1, Called, tells the stories of six people who came to faith as teenagers.

qa.question: Can it be used in a youth group?
qa.answer: Yes. Each chapter can be read in one sitting and ends with four questions written for discussion.

fields.title: Introduction: When Faith Is Tested
fields.body_html:
Some time in the first century, the apostle Peter wrote a letter to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey. They were not famous. Many of them were poor, some were slaves, and all of them were finding out that following Jesus could cost them their friends, their reputations and sometimes far more. Peter did not tell them that their troubles were imaginary, or that they would soon be over. He wrote: “In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:6–7).

Gold is tested by fire: heat it, skim off the rubbish, and what is left is the real thing. Peter’s point was that faith works the same way.

This book is about six people whose faith went through the fire before they were grown up. Some had barely begun to believe when the trouble came; some did not believe at all, and the trouble brought them to God. None of them chose what happened to them. All of them had to choose what to do with it.

Here are the six people you will meet in Tested, the second book of They Were Young:

Patrick, a careless British teenager who was kidnapped by raiders at sixteen, spent six years as a slave herding animals in Ireland, and found God on a cold hillside there.

Josephine Bakhita, a girl from Darfur in Sudan who was stolen from her village as a child and sold again and again, and who, as a young woman in Italy, heard of a Master who was good, and refused to go back to being anyone’s property.

Perpetua, a young mother of about twenty-two in Roman North Africa who kept a diary in prison while her own father begged her to deny Christ and save her life.

The Uganda Martyrs, a group of young men and boys, many of them pages at the court of the king of Buganda in East Africa, who were put to death in the 1880s rather than give up Jesus.

John Newton, a rebellious young sailor who was forced into the navy at eighteen and who, at twenty-two, cried out to God in a storm that nearly sank his ship, but whose story did not end tidily there.

Sundar Singh, a Sikh boy in India who burned a Bible at fifteen because he was so angry with God, and who, a few days later, met the Jesus he had been fighting.

How each chapter works

Each chapter begins with a moment, a decisive scene in that person’s young life, and then pulls back to tell you how they got there and what came after. The rest of the life is told more briefly at the end.

After the story come three short sections. In Their Own Words gives you a few lines the person really said or wrote, with the source. Think It Through offers some questions to wrestle with, alone or with others. Read More on Ochorus points you to the person’s own writing, or their biography, if you want to go further.

One promise about these stories: they are true, and we have tried hard not to add anything to them. We have not invented conversations or made up scenes. Where the old records are silent, or where historians disagree about a date or a detail, we tell you. Some of these people lived so long ago that legends have grown up around them, stories told centuries later that are more famous than the facts. Where that has happened, we say which is which. The real stories are better anyway.

For parents, teachers and youth leaders

These stories are written for readers aged about thirteen to seventeen, and the theme of this book means they go to hard places. They include kidnapping, slavery, imprisonment, persecution and martyrdom, and two of them involve the deaths of young people for their faith. We have handled all of this honestly but without graphic detail. Cruelty is named, not described; slavery and abuse are called what they are, but no story dwells on them.

The chapters work well for discussion, and the Think It Through questions are meant to open conversation rather than settle it. Several raise questions young people really do ask: why God allows suffering, and whether to forgive people who have done terrible things. You do not need to have read the first book in the series, Called, to use this one. Each chapter stands on its own.

fields.title: Patrick: The Slave Who Prayed in the Snow
fields.body_html:
The boy on the hillside was hungry, and he was cold, and he was a long way from home.

He was somewhere in Ireland, around sixteen or seventeen years old, minding animals that belonged to another man. He had no shoes worth the name, no proper coat, and no way of getting home. Home was across the sea, in Britain, and he did not even know which direction to walk. Every morning, before it was light, he got up and went out to the flocks. And every morning, before he did anything else, he prayed.

That is the strange part. A year or two earlier, he would not have bothered. He had grown up in a Christian family, the son of a church deacon and the grandson of a priest, and by his own account he had paid almost no attention to God at all. Now, alone on the hills, he prayed constantly. In his Confession, written many years later, he said that the love of God and the fear of God grew in him more and more, and his faith grew, so that in a single day he would say “as many as a hundred prayers,” and nearly as many at night. He stayed out in the woods and on the mountain, he said, and got up to pray before dawn, “in snow, in frost, in rain,” and he felt no harm from it.

His name was Patrick. Today there are parades in his honour all over the world. On that hillside he was nobody: a slave boy at the edge of the known world. Everything we know about the best part of his story we know because, as an old man, he sat down and wrote it out himself.

A Boy Who Did Not Know God

Patrick lived roughly 1,600 years ago, in the fifth century after Christ. We cannot be more exact than that. The old Irish books give dates for his life, and the year 432 is often named as the year he began his mission in Ireland, but historians have argued about those dates for centuries and many think they were worked out long after he died. What we can say is that he lived as the Roman Empire was falling apart in the west.

For about four hundred years, much of Britain had been part of that empire, and by Patrick’s time it had churches, priests and bishops. But the Roman armies had been pulled out to defend the empire elsewhere, and the coasts of Britain were open to raiders from across the sea.

Patrick tells us where he came from in the first lines of his Confession. His father was named Calpornius, and he was a deacon in the church. His grandfather, Potitus, was a priest. (In those days, clergy in the western church were often married.) In his other surviving writing, a letter, Patrick adds that his father was also a decurion, a member of the local town council, which means the family were fairly well off and important in their community. They lived near a place Patrick calls Bannavem Taburniae, where his father had a small estate. Nobody today knows where that was. Many places have been suggested; none has been proved.

So Patrick was a comfortable boy from a church family. And he was, he says, careless about all of it. He tells us bluntly: “I did not know the true God.” He means that he knew about God, as children of church families always do, but that God meant nothing to him. He says that he and the people around him had turned away from God, did not keep his commandments, and did not listen to the priests who warned them.

He also tells us, much later in his Confession, about something he did when he was about fifteen. He does not say what it was. He only says that it was done in a single hour, that he was not yet strong, and that it weighed on him for years afterwards. We do not know what it was. What matters is that Patrick never pretended to have been a good boy who simply got better. He described himself, over and over, as a sinner who did not deserve what God gave him.

Taken

And then, when he was about sixteen, the raiders came.

Patrick says almost nothing about the attack itself. He says only that he was taken captive and carried off to Ireland “with many thousands of people.” The number may be a rough guess. It may be the way it felt. But the raids of those years were real and terrible, and Irish chieftains brought home captives from Britain to be sold as slaves.

Try to imagine it from the inside. One day you are the son of a respected family, with plans for your future. A few days later you are on a boat, being taken across the sea to a country whose language you do not speak, to be sold.

Ireland in Patrick’s time was not part of the Roman world. It was a land of small kingdoms, each with its own king and cattle. Its people worshipped many gods, and the druids, their priests and wise men, held great power. There may have been a few Christians in Ireland already, and we know that around this time a bishop named Palladius was sent to them from Rome. But for a British teenager, Ireland was the end of the world. Patrick uses that phrase himself again and again: Ireland was, to him, “the ends of the earth.”

Patrick seems to have taken the disaster as God’s judgement, and he did not argue with it. He wrote that he and the others deserved it, because they had turned away from God. That is a hard thing for a modern reader to hear. It does not mean that every terrible thing that happens to a person is a punishment. Years later, as we will see, he was furious with men who did exactly the same thing to others. But looking back on his own life, he believed God had used the worst thing that ever happened to him to wake him up.

Six Years on the Hills

Patrick was put to work looking after animals. He uses a Latin word that can mean sheep, cattle or pigs, so we cannot be sure which. For the next six years, that was his life.

Where in Ireland was he? Later tradition says he worked on a hill called Slemish, in what is now County Antrim, in the north-east of the island. But that tradition comes from a life of Patrick written about two hundred years after his death. In his own Confession, Patrick mentions a place called the Wood of Foclut, “near the western sea,” which many think was in County Mayo, on the opposite side of the island. Historians still argue about whether he was held in the west or the north-east. Again, we simply do not know.

What we do know is what went on inside him. Here is how Patrick describes it in his Confession, in an old English translation: “the Lord opened the understanding of my unbelief” so that, even though late, he might remember his sins and turn with all his heart to God. Notice what he says God did. He did not say that he found God. He said that God opened something in him that had been shut.

And then he tells us what he came to see about God. God, he says, had looked on his low state, and had “pitied the youth of my ignorance,” and had guarded him even before he knew God, and had comforted him “as a father would his son.” This is the heart of Patrick’s story. Alone, unwanted and owned by a stranger, he discovered that he was not alone and not unwanted. He had a Father. The God he had ignored in his comfortable home had not ignored him, and had been looking after him the whole time.

That is when the praying began. A hundred prayers a day and nearly as many at night: the number is surely not a careful count, but it tells you how it felt. He was not praying because someone made him. He was praying because he had found someone to talk to. In snow and frost and rain, before the sun came up, a slave boy on an Irish hillside was getting to know God.

It was not peaceful. He was a slave, often hungry, and he did not know whether he would ever be free. His faith grew in the middle of that, not after it. Many people think faith grows best when life is easy. Patrick’s grew best when he had nothing else.

“Your Ship Is Ready”

After six years, when Patrick was about twenty-two, something happened one night as he slept. He heard a voice, he says, telling him that he was right to fast, and that he would soon go home to his own country. A little while later he heard the voice again: “Look, your ship is ready.”

The ship, he says, was not close. It was perhaps two hundred miles away, in a place he had never been and where he did not know a single person. A runaway slave travelling that far on foot could easily have been caught, and runaways were not treated gently. Patrick went anyway. He walked away from the man he had served for six years, and, as he tells it, he went in the strength of God, who guided his way, and he was afraid of nothing until he reached the ship.

The ship was there. It was about to sail. But when Patrick asked the captain to take him, the captain refused, angrily, and told him he could not come. Patrick does not say why.

Patrick turned away to go back to the little hut where he had been staying, and as he went, he began to pray. Before he had finished the prayer, he heard one of the sailors shouting after him: come back, they would take him after all. The sailors were pagans, and they apparently wanted him to seal his friendship with them by a pagan custom. Patrick refused, hoping instead that they would come to faith in Christ. They let him on board anyway, and they sailed.

Hungry in an Empty Land

The voyage took three days. Then they came to land, but not to home. Patrick does not say where. Some think it was Britain, some think it was Gaul (roughly modern France), where the wars of those years had left whole regions empty. What he does say is that they then travelled for twenty-eight days through a deserted country, and their food ran out.

Patrick tells the next part carefully, and he clearly remembered it well. The captain came to him and said, in effect: you are a Christian; you say your God is great and powerful; why don’t you pray for us, since we are about to starve? Patrick told them to turn to the Lord with all their hearts, because nothing was impossible for him, and that God would send them food that day.

And, Patrick says, a herd of pigs appeared on the road in front of them. The men killed many of them, stayed there two nights, ate their fill, and recovered their strength. After that, he says, they thanked God, and Patrick became respected in their eyes.

Patrick told it plainly, many years later, in a document written to defend his honesty, and he was not a man who liked to boast. He believed that God had heard his prayer, among men who did not share his faith.

Home, and Not Home

Patrick does not tell us how long it took, but eventually, “after a few years,” as he puts it, he was back in Britain with his family. They welcomed him as a son, and they begged him, after everything he had been through, never to leave them again.

You might expect that to be the end of the story.

But one night, Patrick had another dream. He saw a man named Victoricus, coming as if from Ireland, carrying more letters than anyone could count. The man gave Patrick one of them, and he read the first line of it: “The Voice of the Irish.” And as he was reading, he says, he seemed to hear the voices of people who lived beside the Wood of Foclut, near the western sea, crying out together, as if with one voice: “We beseech thee, holy youth, to come and walk again amongst us.” Patrick says he was so moved that he could not read any further, and he woke up.

That dream may remind you of one the apostle Paul had, when he saw a man of Macedonia “standing and pleading with him, ‘Come over to Macedonia and help us’” (Acts 16:9). Patrick certainly knew that story. But think about what his dream asked of him. The Irish were the people who had stolen six years of his life. Ireland was the place where he had been a slave. And the voice was asking him to go back, not as a slave this time, but as a messenger of the God who had found him there. He would have to go back freely, by choice.

He did not go at once. Patrick hints that he was slow to understand what God was doing in him, and the path was not easy. Because he had been kidnapped at sixteen, his education had been cut short just when other young men of his class were studying Latin and rhetoric. For the rest of his life he was embarrassed by his writing. He opens his Confession by calling himself the most unlearned of men, and in his letter he begins: “I, Patrick, a sinner, unlearned, resident in Ireland, declare myself to be a bishop.” He felt that the educated churchmen of Britain looked down on him, and some of them did.

At some point Patrick was trained for the ministry and ordained, first as a deacon and later as a bishop. Old tradition says he studied in Gaul, and Patrick himself mentions that he longed to visit “the brethren” there. But he gives no details, and the timing is uncertain. What we know for certain is the end of the journey: Patrick went back to Ireland, as a bishop, and he never came home to Britain again.

Back to the Ends of the Earth

The rest of Patrick’s life we know only in outline, and almost entirely from his own two short writings.

He travelled through Ireland preaching about Jesus, in a land where nobody was obliged to listen to him and many had good reason to want him gone. He baptized, he says, many thousands of people. He ordained clergy to lead the new churches. He paid the kings whose lands he passed through for safe conduct, because there was no Roman law to protect him. More than once he was seized and threatened. On one occasion, he says, he and his companions were captured and he was kept in chains for fourteen days, expecting to be killed, until he was set free. He wrote that he expected every day to be killed, or betrayed, or taken back into slavery, and that he feared none of it, because of the promises of heaven.

He was particularly moved by the people at the bottom: slaves, and especially enslaved women, who he said suffered the most, and who came to faith in Christ in spite of threats and beatings from those who owned them. He knew what it was like to be in their position.

Patrick was also strict with himself about money. He refused gifts, even the little ornaments that grateful women laid on the altar, and he insisted that he had never charged anyone for baptizing or ordaining them. He wanted no one to be able to say that he had come to Ireland to get rich.

But the hardest opposition did not come from the Irish. It came from other Christians. A group of senior church leaders, probably in Britain, brought charges against him, and as part of their case they dug up the sin he had committed at fifteen. He had told it, years before, to his closest friend, before he was made a deacon. That friend had once supported him strongly. Now, some thirty years after the sin itself, it was used against him. Patrick was deeply hurt. Much of the Confession was written to answer his critics. It is not a boastful defence. Again and again he says that he does not deserve anything, that everything good in his life came from God, and that God had chosen a nobody like him precisely so that no one could doubt it was God’s work.

Then there was Coroticus. He was a British warlord, a man who called himself a Christian, and his soldiers raided the Irish coast, killing some of Patrick’s newly baptized converts and carrying others off to be sold as slaves. Patrick wrote that it happened the day after the converts had been baptized, while they were still wearing the white clothes given to new believers. A sixteen-year-old British boy had once been carried off to Ireland as a slave. Now British raiders were doing the same thing to Irish believers. Patrick wrote a furious public letter, the Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus, demanding that the captives be freed and declaring that Coroticus and his men were cut off from the fellowship of the church until they repented. We do not know whether it worked.

Patrick wrote his Confession in his old age. We do not know when or where he died. Tradition says 17 March, which is why St Patrick’s Day falls on that date, but even the year is disputed. He was probably buried in Ireland, among the people who had once owned him.

What About the Snakes?

You may have heard that Patrick drove all the snakes out of Ireland, or that he explained the Trinity using a shamrock, a little three-leafed clover. These are the most famous things people “know” about him. They are also later legends, and they are not in either of his own writings.

As far as scientists can tell, there were no snakes in Ireland after the last Ice Age, so there were none for him to drive out; the story was told centuries after his death. The shamrock story is later still: it does not seem to appear in writing until more than a thousand years after he lived. Neither is anywhere near as remarkable as what he actually did.

The real Patrick was a careless rich boy who became a slave, a slave who became a man of prayer, and a free man who chose to go back to the people who had enslaved him, to tell them about the God who had found him in their fields. To the end, he called himself a sinner, and he counted it God’s gift that a nobody like him had been sent to the ends of the earth.

In Their Own Words

“He had regard to my low estate, and pitied the youth of my ignorance, and kept me before I knew Him.”

— Patrick, in his Confession (fifth century), in an old English translation

Think It Through

  1. Patrick says that he only really found God after he was kidnapped. Does that mean God caused the kidnapping? How do you think Patrick would answer, and how would you?
  2. When he dreamed of the Irish calling him back, Patrick was being asked to go and serve the people who had enslaved him. What would make that possible for someone? Could you do it?
  3. Some of the hardest opposition Patrick faced came from fellow Christians who brought up a sin he had confessed thirty years earlier. Why do you think that hurt so much, and how should Christians treat someone’s past?
  4. The legends about snakes and shamrocks are far more famous than Patrick’s own words. Why do you think legends grow up around people like him?

Read More on Ochorus

Patrick’s own writings are not yet in the Ochorus library. Both are short: his Confession can be read in under an hour, and it is the best way to meet him. If you want to read another honest, prayerful life story from the same era, written by a man who also came to God after running from him, try Confessions by Augustine of Hippo, written a few decades before Patrick wrote his.

What matters is that Patrick never pretended to have been a good boy who simply got better. He described himself, over and over, as a sinner who did not deserve what God gave him. Taken And then, when he was about sixteen, the raiders came. Patrick says almost nothing about the attack itself. He says only that he was taken captive and carried off to Ireland “with many thousands of people.” The number may be a rough guess. It may be the way it felt. But the raids of those years were real and terrible, and Irish chieftains brought home captives from Britain to be sold as slaves. Try to imagine it from the inside. One day you are the son of a respected family, with plans for your future. A few days later you are on a boat, being taken across the sea to a country whose language you do not speak, to be sold. Ireland in Patrick’s time was not part of the Roman world. It was a land of small kingdoms, each with its own king and cattle. Its people worshipped many gods, and the druids, their priests and wise men, held great power. There may have been a few Christians in Ireland already, and we know that around this time a bishop named Palladius was sent to them from Rome. But for a British teenager, Ireland was the end of the world. Patrick uses that phrase himself again and again: Ireland was, to him, “the ends of the earth.” Patrick seems to have taken the disaster as God’s judgement, and he did not argue with it. He wrote that he and the others deserved it, because they had turned away from God. That is a hard thing for a modern reader to hear. It does not mean that every terrible thing that happens to a person is a punishment. Years later, as we will see, he was furious with men who did exactly the same thing to others. But looking back on his own life, he believed God had used the worst thing that ever happened to him to wake him up. Six Years on the Hills Patrick was put to work looking after animals. He uses a Latin word that can mean sheep, cattle or pigs, so we cannot be sure which. For the next six years, that was his life. Where in Ireland was he? Later tradition says he worked on a hill called Slemish, in what is now County Antrim, in the north-east of the island. But that tradition comes from a life of Patrick written about two hundred years after his death. In his own Confession, Patrick mentions a place called the Wood of Foclut, “near the western sea,” which many think was in County Mayo, on the opposite side of the island. Historians still argue about whether he was held in the west or the north-east. Again, we simply do not know. What we do know is what went on inside him. Here is how Patrick describes it in his Confession, in an old English translation: “the Lord opened the understanding of my unbelief” so that, even though late, he might remember his sins and turn with all his heart to God. Notice what he says God did. He did not say that he found God. He said that God opened something in him that had been shut. And then he tells us what he came to see about God. God, he says, had looked on his low state, and had “pitied the youth of my ignorance,” and had guarded him even before he knew God, and had comforted him “as a father would his son.” This is the heart of Patrick’s story. Alone, unwanted and owned by a stranger, he discovered that he was not alone and not unwanted. He had a Father. The God he had ignored in his comfortable home had not ignored him, and had been looking after him the whole time. That is when the praying began. A hundred prayers a day and nearly as many at night: the number is surely not a careful count, but it tells you how it felt. He was not praying because someone made him. He was praying because he had found someone to talk to. In snow and frost and rain, before the sun came up, a slave boy on an Irish hillside was getting to know God. It was not peaceful. He was a slave, often hungry, and he did not know whether he would ever be free. His faith grew in the middle of that, not after it. Many people think faith grows best when life is easy. Patrick’s grew best when he had nothing else. “Your Ship Is Ready” After six years, when Patrick was about twenty-two, something happened one night as he slept. He heard a voice, he says, telling him that he was right to fast, and that he would soon go home to his own country. A little while later he heard the voice again: “Look, your ship is ready.” The ship, he says, was not close. It was perhaps two hundred miles away, in a place he had never been and where he did not know a single person. A runaway slave travelling that far on foot could easily have been caught, and runaways were not treated gently. Patrick went anyway. He walked away from the man he had served for six years, and, as he tells it, he went in the strength of God, who guided his way, and he was afraid of nothing until he reached the ship. The ship was there. It was about to sail. But when Patrick asked the captain to take him, the captain refused, angrily, and told him he could not come. Patrick does not say why. Patrick turned away to go back to the little hut where he had been staying, and as he went, he began to pray. Before he had finished the prayer, he heard one of the sailors shouting after him: come back, they would take him after all. The sailors were pagans, and they apparently wanted him to seal his friendship with them by a pagan custom. Patrick refused, hoping instead that they would come to faith in Christ. They let him on board anyway, and they sailed. Hungry in an Empty Land The voyage took three days. Then they came to land, but not to home. Patrick does not say where. Some think it was Britain, some think it was Gaul (roughly modern France), where the wars of those years had left whole regions empty. What he does say is that they then travelled for twenty-eight days through a deserted country, and their food ran out. Patrick tells the next part carefully, and he clearly remembered it well. The captain came to him and said, in effect: you are a Christian; you say your God is great and powerful; why don’t you pray for us, since we are about to starve? Patrick told them to turn to the Lord with all their hearts, because nothing was impossible for him, and that God would send them food that day. And, Patrick says, a herd of pigs appeared on the road in front of them. The men killed many of them, stayed there two nights, ate their fill, and recovered their strength. After that, he says, they thanked God, and Patrick became respected in their eyes. Patrick told it plainly, many years later, in a document written to defend his honesty, and he was not a man who liked to boast. He believed that God had heard his prayer, among men who did not share his faith. Home, and Not Home Patrick does not tell us how long it took, but eventually, “after a few years,” as he puts it, he was back in Britain with his family. They welcomed him as a son, and they begged him, after everything he had been through, never to leave them again. You might expect that to be the end of the story. But one night, Patrick had another dream. He saw a man named Victoricus, coming as if from Ireland, carrying more letters than anyone could count. The man gave Patrick one of them, and he read the first line of it: “The Voice of the Irish.” And as he was reading, he says, he seemed to hear the voices of people who lived beside the Wood of Foclut, near the western sea, crying out together, as if with one voice: “We beseech thee, holy youth, to come and walk again amongst us.” Patrick says he was so moved that he could not read any further, and he woke up. That dream may remind you of one the apostle Paul had, when he saw a man of Macedonia “standing and pleading with him, ‘Come over to Macedonia and help us’” (Acts 16:9). Patrick certainly knew that story. But think about what his dream asked of him. The Irish were the people who had stolen six years of his life. Ireland was the place where he had been a slave. And the voice was asking him to go back, not as a slave this time, but as a messenger of the God who had found him there. He would have to go back freely, by choice. He did not go at once. Patrick hints that he was slow to understand what God was doing in him, and the path was not easy. Because he had been kidnapped at sixteen, his education had been cut short just when other young men of his class were studying Latin and rhetoric. For the rest of his life he was embarrassed by his writing. He opens his Confession by calling himself the most unlearned of men, and in his letter he begins: “I, Patrick, a sinner, unlearned, resident in Ireland, declare myself to be a bishop.” He felt that the educated churchmen of Britain looked down on him, and some of them did. At some point Patrick was trained for the ministry and ordained, first as a deacon and later as a bishop. Old tradition says he studied in Gaul, and Patrick himself mentions that he longed to visit “the brethren” there. But he gives no details, and the timing is uncertain. What we know for certain is the end of the journey: Patrick went back to Ireland, as a bishop, and he never came home to Britain again. Back to the Ends of the Earth The rest of Patrick’s life we know only in outline, and almost entirely from his own two short writings. He travelled through Ireland preaching about Jesus, in a land where nobody was obliged to listen to him and many had good reason to want him gone. He baptized, he says, many thousands of people. He ordained clergy to lead the new churches. He paid the kings whose lands he passed through for safe conduct, because there was no Roman law to protect him. More than once he was seized and threatened. On one occasion, he says, he and his companions were captured and he was kept in chains for fourteen days, expecting to be killed, until he was set free. He wrote that he expected every day to be killed, or betrayed, or taken back into slavery, and that he feared none of it, because of the promises of heaven. He was particularly moved by the people at the bottom: slaves, and especially enslaved women, who he said suffered the most, and who came to faith in Christ in spite of threats and beatings from those who owned them. He knew what it was like to be in their position. Patrick was also strict with himself about money. He refused gifts, even the little ornaments that grateful women laid on the altar, and he insisted that he had never charged anyone for baptizing or ordaining them. He wanted no one to be able to say that he had come to Ireland to get rich. But the hardest opposition did not come from the Irish. It came from other Christians. A group of senior church leaders, probably in Britain, brought charges against him, and as part of their case they dug up the sin he had committed at fifteen. He had told it, years before, to his closest friend, before he was made a deacon. That friend had once supported him strongly. Now, some thirty years after the sin itself, it was used against him. Patrick was deeply hurt. Much of the Confession was written to answer his critics. It is not a boastful defence. Again and again he says that he does not deserve anything, that everything good in his life came from God, and that God had chosen a nobody like him precisely so that no one could doubt it was God’s work. Then there was Coroticus. He was a British warlord, a man who called himself a Christian, and his soldiers raided the Irish coast, killing some of Patrick’s newly baptized converts and carrying others off to be sold as slaves. Patrick wrote that it happened the day after the converts had been baptized, while they were still wearing the white clothes given to new believers. A sixteen-year-old British boy had once been carried off to Ireland as a slave. Now British raiders were doing the same thing to Irish believers. Patrick wrote a furious public letter, the Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus, demanding that the captives be freed and declaring that Coroticus and his men were cut off from the fellowship of the church until they repented. We do not know whether it worked. Patrick wrote his Confession in his old age. We do not know when or where he died. Tradition says 17 March, which is why St Patrick’s Day falls on that date, but even the year is disputed. He was probably buried in Ireland, among the people who had once owned him. What About the Snakes? You may have heard that Patrick drove all the snakes out of Ireland, or that he explained the Trinity using a shamrock, a little three-leafed clover. These are the most famous things people “know” about him. They are also later legends, and they are not in either of his own writings. As far as scientists can tell, there were no snakes in Ireland after the last Ice Age, so there were none for him to drive out; the story was told centuries after his death. The shamrock story is later still: it does not seem to appear in writing until more than a thousand years after he lived. Neither is anywhere near as remarkable as what he actually did. The real Patrick was a careless rich boy who became a slave, a slave who became a man of prayer, and a free man who chose to go back to the people who had enslaved him, to tell them about the God who had found him in their fields. To the end, he called himself a sinner, and he counted it God’s gift that a nobody like him had been sent to the ends of the earth. In Their Own Words “He had regard to my low estate, and pitied the youth of my ignorance, and kept me before I knew Him.” — Patrick, in his Confession (fifth century), in an old English translation Think It Through Patrick says that he only really found God after he was kidnapped. Does that mean God caused the kidnapping? How do you think Patrick would answer, and how would you? When he dreamed of the Irish calling him back, Patrick was being asked to go and serve the people who had enslaved him. What would make that possible for someone? Could you do it? Some of the hardest opposition Patrick faced came from fellow Christians who brought up a sin he had confessed thirty years earlier. Why do you think that hurt so much, and how should Christians treat someone’s past? The legends about snakes and shamrocks are far more famous than Patrick’s own words. Why do you think legends grow up around people like him? Read More on Ochorus Patrick’s own writings are not yet in the Ochorus library. Both are short: his Confession can be read in under an hour, and it is the best way to meet him. If you want to read another honest, prayerful life story from the same era, written by a man who also came to God after running from him, try Confessions by Augustine of Hippo, written a few decades before Patrick wrote his.

fields.title: Josephine Bakhita: The Girl Who Said No
fields.body_html:
In the late autumn of 1889, in the city of Venice in northern Italy, a young African woman did something no one had ever allowed her to do. She said no.

She was about twenty years old. Nobody knew her exact age, including her. She was living with a community of religious sisters, women who had given their lives to serving God, at a house they ran in Venice for people who wanted to learn about the Christian faith. She had been brought there about a year earlier by the Italian woman who considered herself her owner, and who had left her there for a time while she went abroad. Now that woman had come back, ready to take her to Africa. Everyone expected that the young woman would go, because she had always gone where she was told. She had been bought and sold, given away and passed from house to house, since she was a small child.

This time she refused. With a firmness that surprised everyone who saw it, she said that she would not leave. She wanted to stay with the sisters, and with the God she had come to know among them.

For three days the woman who considered herself her owner tried to make her change her mind, and the argument grew bitter. The head of the sisters’ house asked the most senior churchman in Venice for help, and the case was taken to the Italian authorities. On 29 November 1889 they gave their answer. The young woman had never legally been a slave in Italy at all. She was free.

Her name, or the name she had been given, was Bakhita. To understand why she said no, you need to know where she had come from, and what she had heard in Venice that made her brave enough to say it.

The Name She Forgot

Bakhita was born in Darfur, in the west of what is now the country of Sudan, in north-east Africa, around 1869. Her village was called Olgossa, and her people were the Daju. Her father was a respected man, the brother of the village chief, and she had three brothers and three sisters. Much later, when she dictated the story of her life, she began with that home. She remembered that she had lived a very happy and carefree life there, “without knowing what suffering was.”

That ended when she was perhaps eight or nine years old, around 1877. Slave raiders had already carried off her eldest sister. Then, one day while Bakhita was out near her village with a friend, two armed strangers seized her and took her away.

In the nineteenth century, a cruel slave trade still operated across this part of Africa. Raiders captured children and adults from villages like hers and marched them to market towns, where they were sold to work in households, on farms or in armies, in Sudan, Egypt and beyond. Many died on the way. Most never saw their families again. Bakhita never did.

She was so frightened that something extraordinary happened to her: she forgot her own name. The account written down by the sisters she later lived with says that the terror drove her name out of her memory, and she was never able to recover it. The name she carried for the rest of her life was the one her captors gave her: Bakhita. It is an Arabic word, and it means “fortunate,” or “lucky.”

It is hard to imagine a crueller name to give a stolen child. Whoever chose it probably meant nothing by it at all. But keep it in mind. By the end of her life, Bakhita had come to believe it was true, though not in any way her kidnappers could have imagined.

Sold, and Sold Again

Bakhita was marched barefoot a very long way, towards the town of El Obeid, and she was bought and sold twice before she even reached it. Once, she and another girl managed to escape. They ran through the forest at night, frightened of the wild animals and of being found, but they were caught again and sold to someone else.

Over the following years, she was sold again and again. Pope Benedict XVI, who later wrote about her, said that she was sold five times in the slave markets of Sudan. She worked in the households of several owners. Some of them treated her very cruelly. In one house, she was beaten so badly by the son of the family that she could not get up for more than a month.

Her worst years were in the household of a Turkish army officer, where she served his wife and his mother-in-law. She said that she could not remember a single day there without some new wound. It was there that Bakhita and the other girls were deliberately marked with cuts on their skin, made so that they would leave permanent scars. She said that she felt she was going to die. She carried the scars, and the marks of the whip, for the rest of her life.

We are not going to describe any more than that, and Bakhita herself, in later years, did not like to dwell on it. But it is important to say clearly what was done to her, because it was real, and because it is still happening. Millions of people in the world today are held in some form of slavery, including many children. Bakhita’s story does not pretend that slavery was anything other than evil. Nor should we.

The Master of the Stars

And yet something else was happening in Bakhita during those years, something no one could see.

She had never been taught about God. Nobody in the households where she served told her about Jesus. But she later remembered looking up at night, at the sun and the moon and the stars, and asking herself who the master of these beautiful things could be. “And I felt a great desire to see him, to know him and to pay him homage,” she said.

It is a remarkable thing for a child in her situation to have felt. Every master she knew was someone who owned her, someone she feared. And here she was, under the African sky, longing to know the master of the stars, without even knowing whether such a person existed, or whether he would be any kinder than the others.

The Bible says something similar. The heavens declare the glory of God, Psalm 19 says, and the apostle Paul wrote that God’s eternal power and divine nature can be clearly seen in what he has made. Bakhita did not know any of those verses. She simply looked up, and wondered.

A Different Kind of Master

In the early 1880s, a great uprising swept across Sudan, led by a religious leader called the Mahdi, against the Egyptian government that ruled the region. As the fighting came closer, Bakhita’s owner, the Turkish officer, decided to leave, and he sold most of his slaves. In Khartoum, the capital, around 1882, Bakhita was bought by an Italian diplomat named Callisto Legnani, the Italian consul.

Bakhita was about thirteen. And she noticed something at once. In Legnani’s house, no one used the whip when they gave her orders. For the first time since she had been taken from her village, she was treated kindly. She later remembered peace in that house, and even happiness, though it was mixed with grief for the family she would never see again.

She was still not free. Legnani had bought her, and in Sudan she was still considered property. But over the next two years she was safe. Then the war reached Khartoum, and Legnani had to flee. Bakhita begged him to take her with him, and he agreed. They crossed the desert by camel to the port of Suakin on the Red Sea, took a ship, and in 1885 arrived in Genoa, in Italy. She was about sixteen.

In Italy, Legnani gave Bakhita to a friend’s wife, Signora Michieli, and Bakhita went with the Michieli family to their country house near the village of Mirano, near Venice. When the Michielis’ daughter Alice, nicknamed Mimmina, was born in 1886, Bakhita became her nanny. She loved the little girl, and Mimmina loved her.

“Who Is This?”

Around this time, the man who managed the Michieli family’s property, Illuminato Checchini, gave Bakhita a small silver crucifix: a cross with the figure of Jesus on it. As she later remembered it, he kissed it and explained that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, had died for us. She did not understand what that meant. But she kept the little cross, and she looked at it often, secretly, and wondered about it. Who was this man who had suffered like that?

In 1888 the Michielis decided to move to Africa for good. Augusto Michieli had bought a hotel in Suakin, the same port Bakhita had sailed from. While the family’s Italian property was being sold, Signora Michieli needed somewhere safe to leave Mimmina and her nanny. On Checchini’s advice, she placed them both with the Canossian Sisters, an order of women devoted to teaching and caring for the poor, at the house they ran in Venice for people preparing to become Christians. Bakhita arrived there in late November 1888.

And there, at last, someone explained to her what the cross meant.

The sisters taught her about God. She later said that they introduced her to “that God who from childhood I had felt in my heart without knowing who He was.” The master of the stars had a name. And he was not like any master she had ever known.

Bakhita learned the dialect of Venice, and in that dialect the word for the master of a household is “paron.” It was the word she came to use for God. All her life she had known masters who despised her, who beat her, or at best found her useful. Now she heard of a Paron above every master, who had made her, who knew her and loved her, and who had sent his Son, Jesus, to live and die for her. She learned that Jesus himself had been stripped, beaten and whipped, like a slave. He had been nailed to a cross, the very thing on the little silver crucifix she had kept. And he had died there for the sins of the world, and risen again, and was waiting to welcome her as his own.

For a girl who had been owned, that changed everything. The Bible says that Christians did not “receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear,” but the Spirit by whom they cry out to God, “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15). Bakhita had been a slave since childhood. Now she was being told that she could be a daughter.

Free

That is why, when Signora Michieli came back to Venice towards the end of 1889 to take her to Africa, Bakhita said no.

It was not that she was ungrateful. She was fond of the family, and leaving Mimmina was painful. But she had found something she could not leave behind, and she knew that in Africa she would have no chance to be baptized, or to learn more about the Lord she had come to love. It was the first time in her life that she had refused to obey someone who claimed to own her, and she did it calmly, firmly, and without backing down.

Signora Michieli was furious, and for three days she tried to change Bakhita’s mind and to take her by force. The sisters’ superior appealed to the Patriarch of Venice, the senior church leader in the city, and the matter was passed to the state authorities. The answer they gave on 29 November 1889 was simple. Slavery had already been outlawed in Sudan before Bakhita was born, and Italian law had never recognized slavery at all. In the eyes of the law, she had never been anyone’s property. She was free to go wherever she wanted.

She chose to stay.

On 9 January 1890, at about twenty years old, Bakhita was baptized. She took the name Josephine. For years afterwards, people saw her kissing the baptismal font, the basin of water where she had been baptized, and saying, “Here, I became a daughter of God!”

Think about what had happened. Her kidnappers had taken her name and her family and her childhood. They had given her a new name as if she were an animal. Now, freely, she received another name, as a daughter, from a Father who would never sell her and never let her go.

Madre Moretta

Freedom did not send Josephine Bakhita away from the sisters. It drew her closer to them. She felt that God was calling her to give her whole life to him, and in December 1893 she began training to become a Canossian sister herself. On 8 December 1896, in the city of Verona, she made her vows. On that day she prayed that she might fly south to her own people in Africa and tell them loudly of God’s goodness, and she prayed especially for her mother and father, her brothers, and her sister, who she believed was still a slave.

She never did go back to Africa. In 1902 she was sent to the Canossian convent in Schio, a small industrial town in the foothills of the Alps, and apart from a few years away she lived there for the rest of her life. Her work was the plainest work a convent has: she cooked, she sewed and embroidered, she looked after the church, and for many years she was the doorkeeper, greeting everyone who came. She would gently lay her hands on the heads of the children arriving each day at the convent’s school. During the First World War, part of the convent became a military hospital, and she helped to care for the wounded.

The people of Schio came to love her. Many of them had probably never seen an African person before. They called her Madre Moretta, “our black mother,” and they meant it with affection. They remembered her gentleness, her smile and her short, simple advice: be good, love the Lord, pray for those who do not know him.

In 1910, at her superiors’ request, she told the story of her life, and it was written down. In 1931 it was published in Italy, and she became famous. For several years in the late 1930s she travelled around Italy to tell her story and help prepare young sisters going to Africa as missionaries. People often asked her the hardest question of all: what would she do if she ever met the people who had kidnapped and tortured her? She answered that she would kneel and kiss their hands, because if those things had not happened, she would never have become a Christian. It is easy to misread that. She was not saying that slavery was good, or that the slavers had done well. She was refusing to hate them, and refusing to let them have the last word on her life. “Poor things,” she said of them on another occasion. “They did not know the Lord.”

During the Second World War, Schio, as an industrial town, was bombed. The townspeople felt safer with the old African sister among them, and she told them calmly that God was in charge. In her last years she was ill and in pain, and confined to a wheelchair, but when people asked her how she was, she would answer, “As the Master desires.” At the very end, her mind went back to the slave roads of her childhood, and she begged the nurse to loosen the chains on her, because they were heavy. Then the fear passed. She died peacefully at Schio on 8 February 1947, at about seventy-eight years old.

The Catholic Church later declared her a saint, in 2000, and she is remembered especially by people working against human trafficking today. She is honoured as patron of Sudan, the country she was stolen from. But Bakhita herself would have pointed away from herself to her Paron. A stolen girl had been given the name “fortunate” as a cruel joke. At the end of her life, she believed it was the truest thing anyone had ever called her: not because of what had been done to her, but because, in the middle of it, the Master of the stars had found her and called her his daughter.

In Their Own Words

“Seeing the sun, the moon and the stars, I said to myself: Who could be the Master of these beautiful things? And I felt a great desire to see him, to know him and to pay him homage.”

— Josephine Bakhita, remembering her years in slavery, in the story of her life dictated in 1910

Think It Through

  1. Bakhita longed to know the “Master” of the stars long before anyone told her about God. What do you think the world around you says about God, and what can it not say?
  2. Bakhita called God “Paron,” Master, a word that had meant fear and pain for her whole childhood. Why do you think it mattered to her that Jesus himself had been beaten and whipped?
  3. The first time Bakhita refused to obey an owner was when she said no to leaving Venice. What gave her the courage? When does saying no take more courage than saying yes?
  4. Bakhita said she would kiss the hands of the people who had kidnapped her. Is it possible to forgive someone without saying that what they did was all right? What is the difference?

Read More on Ochorus

Josephine Bakhita did not write books, and the story of her life that she dictated is not in the Ochorus library. But her author page carries a full biography, with much more of her own words: about the night sky over Darfur, the day of her baptism, her years at the convent door in Schio and her answer to the question of forgiveness.
