Raiders captured children and adults from villages like hers and marched them to market towns, where they were sold to work in households, on farms or in armies, in Sudan, Egypt and beyond. Many died on the way. Most never saw their families again. Bakhita never did. She was so frightened that something extraordinary happened to her: she forgot her own name. The account written down by the sisters she later lived with says that the terror drove her name out of her memory, and she was never able to recover it. The name she carried for the rest of her life was the one her captors gave her: Bakhita. It is an Arabic word, and it means “fortunate,” or “lucky.” It is hard to imagine a crueller name to give a stolen child. Whoever chose it probably meant nothing by it at all. But keep it in mind. By the end of her life, Bakhita had come to believe it was true, though not in any way her kidnappers could have imagined. Sold, and Sold Again Bakhita was marched barefoot a very long way, towards the town of El Obeid, and she was bought and sold twice before she even reached it. Once, she and another girl managed to escape. They ran through the forest at night, frightened of the wild animals and of being found, but they were caught again and sold to someone else. Over the following years, she was sold again and again. Pope Benedict XVI, who later wrote about her, said that she was sold five times in the slave markets of Sudan. She worked in the households of several owners. Some of them treated her very cruelly. In one house, she was beaten so badly by the son of the family that she could not get up for more than a month. Her worst years were in the household of a Turkish army officer, where she served his wife and his mother-in-law. She said that she could not remember a single day there without some new wound. It was there that Bakhita and the other girls were deliberately marked with cuts on their skin, made so that they would leave permanent scars. She said that she felt she was going to die. She carried the scars, and the marks of the whip, for the rest of her life. We are not going to describe any more than that, and Bakhita herself, in later years, did not like to dwell on it. But it is important to say clearly what was done to her, because it was real, and because it is still happening. Millions of people in the world today are held in some form of slavery, including many children. Bakhita’s story does not pretend that slavery was anything other than evil. Nor should we. The Master of the Stars And yet something else was happening in Bakhita during those years, something no one could see. She had never been taught about God. Nobody in the households where she served told her about Jesus. But she later remembered looking up at night, at the sun and the moon and the stars, and asking herself who the master of these beautiful things could be. “And I felt a great desire to see him, to know him and to pay him homage,” she said. It is a remarkable thing for a child in her situation to have felt. Every master she knew was someone who owned her, someone she feared. And here she was, under the African sky, longing to know the master of the stars, without even knowing whether such a person existed, or whether he would be any kinder than the others. The Bible says something similar. The heavens declare the glory of God, Psalm 19 says, and the apostle Paul wrote that God’s eternal power and divine nature can be clearly seen in what he has made. Bakhita did not know any of those verses. She simply looked up, and wondered. A Different Kind of Master In the early 1880s, a great uprising swept across Sudan, led by a religious leader called the Mahdi, against the Egyptian government that ruled the region. As the fighting came closer, Bakhita’s owner, the Turkish officer, decided to leave, and he sold most of his slaves. In Khartoum, the capital, around 1882, Bakhita was bought by an Italian diplomat named Callisto Legnani, the Italian consul. Bakhita was about thirteen. And she noticed something at once. In Legnani’s house, no one used the whip when they gave her orders. For the first time since she had been taken from her village, she was treated kindly. She later remembered peace in that house, and even happiness, though it was mixed with grief for the family she would never see again. She was still not free. Legnani had bought her, and in Sudan she was still considered property. But over the next two years she was safe. Then the war reached Khartoum, and Legnani had to flee. Bakhita begged him to take her with him, and he agreed. They crossed the desert by camel to the port of Suakin on the Red Sea, took a ship, and in 1885 arrived in Genoa, in Italy. She was about sixteen. In Italy, Legnani gave Bakhita to a friend’s wife, Signora Michieli, and Bakhita went with the Michieli family to their country house near the village of Mirano, near Venice. When the Michielis’ daughter Alice, nicknamed Mimmina, was born in 1886, Bakhita became her nanny. She loved the little girl, and Mimmina loved her. “Who Is This?” Around this time, the man who managed the Michieli family’s property, Illuminato Checchini, gave Bakhita a small silver crucifix: a cross with the figure of Jesus on it. As she later remembered it, he kissed it and explained that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, had died for us. She did not understand what that meant. But she kept the little cross, and she looked at it often, secretly, and wondered about it. Who was this man who had suffered like that? In 1888 the Michielis decided to move to Africa for good. Augusto Michieli had bought a hotel in Suakin, the same port Bakhita had sailed from. While the family’s Italian property was being sold, Signora Michieli needed somewhere safe to leave Mimmina and her nanny. On Checchini’s advice, she placed them both with the Canossian Sisters, an order of women devoted to teaching and caring for the poor, at the house they ran in Venice for people preparing to become Christians. Bakhita arrived there in late November 1888. And there, at last, someone explained to her what the cross meant. The sisters taught her about God. She later said that they introduced her to “that God who from childhood I had felt in my heart without knowing who He was.” The master of the stars had a name. And he was not like any master she had ever known. Bakhita learned the dialect of Venice, and in that dialect the word for the master of a household is “paron.” It was the word she came to use for God. All her life she had known masters who despised her, who beat her, or at best found her useful. Now she heard of a Paron above every master, who had made her, who knew her and loved her, and who had sent his Son, Jesus, to live and die for her. She learned that Jesus himself had been stripped, beaten and whipped, like a slave. He had been nailed to a cross, the very thing on the little silver crucifix she had kept. And he had died there for the sins of the world, and risen again, and was waiting to welcome her as his own. For a girl who had been owned, that changed everything. The Bible says that Christians did not “receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear,” but the Spirit by whom they cry out to God, “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15). Bakhita had been a slave since childhood. Now she was being told that she could be a daughter. Free That is why, when Signora Michieli came back to Venice towards the end of 1889 to take her to Africa, Bakhita said no. It was not that she was ungrateful. She was fond of the family, and leaving Mimmina was painful. But she had found something she could not leave behind, and she knew that in Africa she would have no chance to be baptized, or to learn more about the Lord she had come to love. It was the first time in her life that she had refused to obey someone who claimed to own her, and she did it calmly, firmly, and without backing down. Signora Michieli was furious, and for three days she tried to change Bakhita’s mind and to take her by force. The sisters’ superior appealed to the Patriarch of Venice, the senior church leader in the city, and the matter was passed to the state authorities. The answer they gave on 29 November 1889 was simple. Slavery had already been outlawed in Sudan before Bakhita was born, and Italian law had never recognized slavery at all. In the eyes of the law, she had never been anyone’s property. She was free to go wherever she wanted. She chose to stay. On 9 January 1890, at about twenty years old, Bakhita was baptized. She took the name Josephine. For years afterwards, people saw her kissing the baptismal font, the basin of water where she had been baptized, and saying, “Here, I became a daughter of God!” Think about what had happened. Her kidnappers had taken her name and her family and her childhood. They had given her a new name as if she were an animal. Now, freely, she received another name, as a daughter, from a Father who would never sell her and never let her go. Madre Moretta Freedom did not send Josephine Bakhita away from the sisters. It drew her closer to them. She felt that God was calling her to give her whole life to him, and in December 1893 she began training to become a Canossian sister herself. On 8 December 1896, in the city of Verona, she made her vows. On that day she prayed that she might fly south to her own people in Africa and tell them loudly of God’s goodness, and she prayed especially for her mother and father, her brothers, and her sister, who she believed was still a slave. She never did go back to Africa. In 1902 she was sent to the Canossian convent in Schio, a small industrial town in the foothills of the Alps, and apart from a few years away she lived there for the rest of her life. Her work was the plainest work a convent has: she cooked, she sewed and embroidered, she looked after the church, and for many years she was the doorkeeper, greeting everyone who came. She would gently lay her hands on the heads of the children arriving each day at the convent’s school. During the First World War, part of the convent became a military hospital, and she helped to care for the wounded. The people of Schio came to love her. Many of them had probably never seen an African person before. They called her Madre Moretta, “our black mother,” and they meant it with affection. They remembered her gentleness, her smile and her short, simple advice: be good, love the Lord, pray for those who do not know him. In 1910, at her superiors’ request, she told the story of her life, and it was written down. In 1931 it was published in Italy, and she became famous. For several years in the late 1930s she travelled around Italy to tell her story and help prepare young sisters going to Africa as missionaries. People often asked her the hardest question of all: what would she do if she ever met the people who had kidnapped and tortured her? She answered that she would kneel and kiss their hands, because if those things had not happened, she would never have become a Christian. It is easy to misread that. She was not saying that slavery was good, or that the slavers had done well. She was refusing to hate them, and refusing to let them have the last word on her life. “Poor things,” she said of them on another occasion. “They did not know the Lord.” During the Second World War, Schio, as an industrial town, was bombed. The townspeople felt safer with the old African sister among them, and she told them calmly that God was in charge. In her last years she was ill and in pain, and confined to a wheelchair, but when people asked her how she was, she would answer, “As the Master desires.” At the very end, her mind went back to the slave roads of her childhood, and she begged the nurse to loosen the chains on her, because they were heavy. Then the fear passed. She died peacefully at Schio on 8 February 1947, at about seventy-eight years old. The Catholic Church later declared her a saint, in 2000, and she is remembered especially by people working against human trafficking today. She is honoured as patron of Sudan, the country she was stolen from. But Bakhita herself would have pointed away from herself to her Paron. A stolen girl had been given the name “fortunate” as a cruel joke. At the end of her life, she believed it was the truest thing anyone had ever called her: not because of what had been done to her, but because, in the middle of it, the Master of the stars had found her and called her his daughter. In Their Own Words “Seeing the sun, the moon and the stars, I said to myself: Who could be the Master of these beautiful things? And I felt a great desire to see him, to know him and to pay him homage.” — Josephine Bakhita, remembering her years in slavery, in the story of her life dictated in 1910 Think It Through Bakhita longed to know the “Master” of the stars long before anyone told her about God. What do you think the world around you says about God, and what can it not say? Bakhita called God “Paron,” Master, a word that had meant fear and pain for her whole childhood. Why do you think it mattered to her that Jesus himself had been beaten and whipped? The first time Bakhita refused to obey an owner was when she said no to leaving Venice. What gave her the courage? When does saying no take more courage than saying yes? Bakhita said she would kiss the hands of the people who had kidnapped her. Is it possible to forgive someone without saying that what they did was all right? What is the difference? Read More on Ochorus Josephine Bakhita did not write books, and the story of her life that she dictated is not in the Ochorus library. But her author page carries a full biography, with much more of her own words: about the night sky over Darfur, the day of her baptism, her years at the convent door in Schio and her answer to the question of forgiveness.

fields.title: Perpetua: What a Thing Is Called
fields.body_html:
The young woman had been under arrest for only a few days when her father came to see her. They had not yet been taken to the prison. She was being held under guard somewhere in or near the city of Carthage, in North Africa, in the early spring of the year 203, and her father had come for one reason: to talk her out of it.

Her name was Vibia Perpetua. She was about twenty-two years old. She had a baby son who was still nursing. And she was being held because she would not stop calling herself a Christian.

We know what happened next because Perpetua wrote it down herself. Her father, she says, loved her, and because he loved her he kept on and on at her, trying to turn her away from her faith. So she pointed to a jug that was lying there, a little water-pot, and asked him whether he could see it. He said he could. She asked whether it could be called by any other name than what it was. He said no. And then she gave him her answer. In a well-known old English translation it reads: “Neither can I call myself anything else than what I am, a Christian.”

Her father was so angry that he threw himself at her as if he would tear out her eyes. But he did not hurt her. He only frightened and distressed her, and then he went away, beaten. For a few days afterwards he did not come back, and Perpetua wrote, honestly, that she thanked God for his absence and felt refreshed by it.

It is a small scene: a daughter, a father and a clay jug. But it holds the whole of her story.

A Diary from a Prison

Before we go further, you need to know something unusual about this story. Most of what we know about early Christians who died for their faith comes from other people: friends, church leaders, or writers many years later. Perpetua’s story is different. Large parts of it are in her own words.

The account is called The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. (“Passion” here means suffering, as in the “Passion” of Christ.) It has three layers. In the middle is Perpetua’s own diary, written in prison, in the first person, describing her arrest, her family, her visions and her trial, right up to the day before she died. Next to it is a shorter account of a dream written by Saturus, the man who had taught her the faith. Around both of them is a frame written by an editor, an unnamed Christian in Carthage who gathered the pieces together soon after the martyrs died, added an introduction, and described what happened in the arena, which Perpetua of course could not write herself. Some people have guessed that the editor was the famous Carthaginian writer Tertullian. Nobody knows for certain.

Perpetua’s section is widely thought to be the oldest surviving piece of writing by a Christian woman. Of all the women who followed Jesus in the church’s first two centuries, the first whose own words we can still read was a young mother in a prison, writing in the weeks before her death.

She ended her diary with a sentence that tells you she knew exactly what she was doing. This is what I did, she wrote, up to the day before the games; what happens at the games themselves, let someone else write, if they want to.

Carthage, About the Year 200

Carthage stood on the coast of North Africa, close to where Tunis, in Tunisia, stands today. Once Rome’s great rival, it had been destroyed and rebuilt as a Roman city, and by Perpetua’s time it was one of the largest and richest cities in the western half of the empire, with a huge amphitheatre where crowds watched gladiators and wild animals.

The church in Carthage was growing, and that made people nervous. Christians would not offer sacrifice to the gods of Rome or to the emperor’s well-being, and to many Romans that looked like disloyalty, even a danger to the city. Persecution in this period was not constant everywhere. It came in waves, often stirred up locally. Around 202 and 203, in the reign of the emperor Septimius Severus (who was himself born in North Africa), a wave broke over Carthage.

A few years earlier, Tertullian, who lived in Carthage, had written a bold defence of the Christians addressed to the Roman authorities. Near the end of it he wrote the line he is most remembered for. In the usual English it is: “The blood of Christians is seed.” The more you kill us, he meant, the more of us there will be. Perpetua was about to show what it meant.

Who She Was

The editor tells us that Perpetua was “well born,” well educated, and married in the respectable way. Her father was alive, and so was her mother. She had two brothers, one of them, like her, a catechumen. She had an aunt she mentions once. Her husband is never mentioned at all, not by her and not by the editor. We do not know whether he had died, or left, or simply was not part of the story. It is one of the silences in the account, and it is better to leave it as a silence than to fill it with a guess.

A catechumen was a person who was learning the Christian faith and preparing to be baptized. In the church of that time, preparation could last a long while, and people often waited months or years for baptism. So when Perpetua was arrested, she had not yet been baptized. She was a believer who had not yet gone through the water.

She was not arrested alone. With her were several other young catechumens: two who were slaves, Revocatus and a young woman named Felicity, and two others, Saturninus and Secundulus. Felicity was pregnant, about eight months along. Their teacher, Saturus, was not with them when they were taken. Later, of his own free will, he went to the authorities and gave himself up so that he could share what was happening to the people he had taught.

In Roman society a noblewoman and a pregnant slave would never have sat at the same table. In this account they are simply sisters, and they would die side by side.

The Dark

A few days after the scene with the pitcher, while the father was staying away, the catechumens were baptized. We are not told who baptized them or exactly where. Perpetua tells us only one thing about it: that as she came out of the water, she felt the Spirit prompting her to ask for nothing else from it except endurance in the body. She knew what was coming.

Then they were put in prison, and Perpetua was terrified. She was honest about that. She had never known darkness like it, she wrote. It was crowded and stiflingly hot, and the soldiers pushed the prisoners around and squeezed them for bribes. On top of all of it, she was sick with worry for her baby.

Two deacons of the church, whom she names as Tertius and Pomponius, paid the guards so that the prisoners could spend a few hours in a better part of the prison. There Perpetua nursed her son, who was weak with hunger. She talked with her mother and her brother, and handed the baby to them to look after. She saw how much they were suffering because of her, and she said it hurt her to see it. For several days she lived with that anxiety.

Then she was given permission to keep the baby with her in the prison. And at once, she wrote, she grew strong again. Her worry for him lifted, and her prison suddenly became like a palace to her, so that she would rather be there than anywhere else.

The Ladder

Perpetua’s brother came to her with a request. You are greatly honoured now, he told her (this is her report of what he said, not a word-for-word record), so ask God for a vision, and find out whether this will end in suffering or in release. Perpetua had already found that she could speak with the Lord, and she promised him she would tell him the next day. She asked. And she saw this.

There was a ladder, enormously tall, reaching all the way up to heaven. It was made of bronze, and it was so narrow that only one person could climb it at a time. Fixed to its sides were all kinds of iron weapons: swords, spears, hooks, knives. Anyone who climbed carelessly, without looking up, would be torn by them. And under the ladder lay a huge serpent, waiting to attack anyone who tried to climb and to frighten them off.

Saturus went up first. At the top he turned and called down to her that he was waiting for her, and told her to be careful that the serpent did not bite her. She answered that in the name of Jesus Christ it would not hurt her. And then, she says, the serpent slowly put out its head from under the ladder, as if it were afraid of her, and she used its head as the first step, and climbed.

At the top she saw a huge garden. In the middle of it sat a tall man with white hair, dressed as a shepherd, milking sheep. Around him stood many thousands of people dressed in white. He lifted his head, looked at her, and welcomed her as his child. He gave her a mouthful of the cheese he was making, and she took it in her cupped hands and ate it, and everyone standing round said “Amen.” At that sound she woke up, still tasting something sweet.

She told her brother what she had seen. They both understood what it meant. It would not be release. From then on, she wrote, they stopped hoping in anything this world could give.

Christians have long heard in the trodden serpent’s head an echo of the Bible’s first promise, that the woman’s offspring “will crush your head” (Genesis 3:15). Perpetua did not explain her dream that way herself. But she clearly understood who the shepherd was, who the serpent was, and which of them had already won.

“Have Pity on My Grey Hair”

A rumour went round that the prisoners were going to be given a hearing. Perpetua’s father came in from the city, worn out with grief, and tried one last time.

This time he did not shout. Perpetua records what he said, and it is one of the most painful passages in the whole account. He begged her to have pity on his grey hair. He reminded her that he had raised her, that he had loved her more than her brothers. He asked her to think of her mother and her aunt and her brothers, and of her son, who would not be able to live after she was gone. He told her not to destroy them all. He kissed her hands and threw himself at her feet, weeping, and he no longer called her “daughter” but “lady,” the way a servant would address his mistress.

Perpetua says she was grieved for him, because he was the only one of her whole family who would not be glad at what she was about to suffer. She tried to comfort him. Whatever happened at the trial, she told him, would be what God willed, because, in the old translation, “we are not placed in our own power, but in that of God.” He went away in deep sorrow.

Perpetua was not cold. She grieved over her father on almost every page she wrote about him. But she would not stop being what she was to make the pain stop, even his pain. Jesus had said that anyone who loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:37). Very few people in history have had to live that verse as literally as Perpetua did.

The Hearing

One day, while they were eating, the prisoners were suddenly taken away to the forum, the public square, for their hearing. A huge crowd gathered. The judge was a Roman official named Hilarianus, who was acting governor of the province because the governor had recently died.

One by one the others were questioned, and one by one they confessed that they were Christians. Then it was Perpetua’s turn. At that moment her father appeared, holding her baby son. He pulled her down off the step and begged her to offer the sacrifice and have pity on the child.

Hilarianus joined in. Spare your father’s grey hair, he told her; spare your little boy; offer a sacrifice for the safety of the emperors. It was a small act, and many in the crowd must have thought her mad to refuse.

She said she would not. He asked her plainly whether she was a Christian. And she said that she was.

Her father kept trying to pull her down, and Hilarianus ordered him thrown to the ground and beaten with a rod. Perpetua wrote that she felt it as if she herself had been struck, and that she grieved for him in his miserable old age.

Then Hilarianus sentenced them all to be thrown to the wild beasts in the arena. And Perpetua wrote that they went back down to the prison cheerful.

There was one more sorrow. Her baby had been used to nursing and staying with her in the prison, and she sent the deacon Pomponius to her father to ask for him. Her father refused to give the child back. And then, she says, as God willed it, the baby no longer wanted to nurse, and she was not left in pain or fever. She did not have to be tormented, she wrote, either by worry for the child or by pain in her body. She saw even that as a mercy.

The Last Days

In the days that remained, Perpetua had more visions, two of them bringing her comfort about a little brother, Dinocrates, who had died of a disease at seven. The last came on the day before the games. She dreamed that she was led into the arena and fought not an animal but a frightening man, an Egyptian, and trod on his head, and a tall figure gave her a branch of victory and said, “Peace be with you, daughter.” She woke understanding that she would fight not with beasts but with the devil, and that the victory would be hers.

A military officer in charge of the prison, named Pudens, began to treat the prisoners with respect, because he could see, the editor says, some great power in them. He let their friends visit.

Saturus had his own dream, which the editor included in his words: he and Perpetua were carried by angels into a garden of light, where voices sang “Holy, holy, holy” without end.

The editor also tells us about Felicity. She was by now eight months pregnant, and she was distressed, because Roman law did not allow a pregnant woman to be executed, and she was afraid she would be held back and later put to death among strangers instead of with her friends. Her companions prayed with her, three days before the games. Immediately afterwards her labour began, and she gave birth to a baby girl. It was a hard birth, and she cried out in pain. One of the prison guards mocked her: if this hurts you so much, what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts?

Felicity’s reply has been remembered ever since. In the old translation: “I now suffer that which I suffer; but then there will be another in me, who will suffer for me, because I also am about to suffer for Him.” A Christian woman, one of the “sisters,” took the baby girl and raised her as her own daughter.

Felicity was a slave. Nobody else in Carthage would have thought her words worth writing down. The church did.

The Arena

The editor’s account of the last day, 7 March 203, is honest, and we will be honest too, without lingering.

The prisoners walked from the prison to the amphitheatre, the editor says, as if they were going to heaven, joyful, with calm faces. Perpetua walked steadily, her face shining, singing a psalm. When the officials tried to make them dress in costumes as priests and priestesses of the Roman gods, Perpetua refused: they had come of their own accord, she said, precisely so that they would not have to do such things. The officials gave way.

The men faced leopards, a bear and a boar. Perpetua and Felicity were sent in against a wild cow, and both were knocked down and hurt. The account remembers small, human things about Perpetua in that moment: that she pulled her torn tunic straight to cover herself, that she asked for a pin to put up her hair, and that, seeing Felicity on the ground, she went over, gave her her hand, and helped her up. Afterwards, at the gate, she seemed to come out of a kind of daze and asked when they were going to be sent against the cow. She would not believe it had already happened until she saw the marks on her own body.

Then she called over her brother and another catechumen and said to them, in the old translation: “Stand fast in the faith, and love one another, all of you, and be not offended at my sufferings.”

At the end, the martyrs who were still alive exchanged the kiss of peace with one another, and were put to death by the sword. The editor records that the young gladiator sent to kill Perpetua was inexperienced and his hand shook, and that she herself guided it. Saturus, who had climbed the ladder first in her dream, had died just before her. He had told Pudens, the prison officer, to remember his faith and not to be troubled but strengthened by what he saw. The editor says that Pudens, by then, was a believer.

What Came After

Perpetua and Felicity were not forgotten. Within a few years their story was being read aloud in the churches of North Africa. A generation later, Cyprian became bishop of Carthage and, in 258, was himself martyred there, beheaded under another emperor. Two centuries after Perpetua, the great North African bishop Augustine preached sermons on the day of her and Felicity’s feast, and in another of his writings he reminded readers that, much as they loved the account, it was not Scripture. Their names are still read and honoured on 7 March by Christians in many traditions around the world.

But the most important thing about Perpetua is not her fame. It is the jug. At twenty-two, not yet baptized, with a baby who needed her and a father whose heart she was breaking, she still could not make herself anything other than what she had become: a person who belonged to Jesus Christ, and who believed that he had already crushed the serpent’s head.

In Their Own Words

“We are not placed in our own power, but in that of God.”

— Perpetua, to her father, in The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (203)

Think It Through

  1. Perpetua answered her father with a clay jug: a thing can only be called what it is. What would it mean for you to be “called” a Christian in a place where that costs you something? Where is that hardest for you?
  2. Perpetua loved her father and grieved for him, yet would not do what he asked. How can a person stay loving towards family who oppose their faith, without giving way?
  3. A noblewoman and a slave died side by side, and the slave’s words were written down and remembered. What does that tell you about what the gospel did to the way these Christians saw one another?
  4. Perpetua was honest in her diary about being terrified in the dark prison, and about being relieved when her father stayed away. Does it help you to know that a martyr felt fear? Why might it matter that she did not hide it?

Read More on Ochorus

Perpetua and Felicity appear in Fox’s Book of Martyrs, in the chapter “The Ten Primitive Persecutions,” which tells the story briefly (its date, 205, differs a little from the one most historians give, 203). For the church in Carthage a generation later, read The Treatises of Cyprian, by the bishop who led that same church through another persecution and died for his faith in 258; his author page carries a full biography. Tertullian’s own writings are not yet in the library.

She was being held under guard somewhere in or near the city of Carthage, in North Africa, in the early spring of the year 203, and her father had come for one reason: to talk her out of it. Her name was Vibia Perpetua. She was about twenty-two years old. She had a baby son who was still nursing. And she was being held because she would not stop calling herself a Christian. We know what happened next because Perpetua wrote it down herself. Her father, she says, loved her, and because he loved her he kept on and on at her, trying to turn her away from her faith. So she pointed to a jug that was lying there, a little water-pot, and asked him whether he could see it. He said he could. She asked whether it could be called by any other name than what it was. He said no. And then she gave him her answer. In a well-known old English translation it reads: “Neither can I call myself anything else than what I am, a Christian.” Her father was so angry that he threw himself at her as if he would tear out her eyes. But he did not hurt her. He only frightened and distressed her, and then he went away, beaten. For a few days afterwards he did not come back, and Perpetua wrote, honestly, that she thanked God for his absence and felt refreshed by it. It is a small scene: a daughter, a father and a clay jug. But it holds the whole of her story. A Diary from a Prison Before we go further, you need to know something unusual about this story. Most of what we know about early Christians who died for their faith comes from other people: friends, church leaders, or writers many years later. Perpetua’s story is different. Large parts of it are in her own words. The account is called The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. (“Passion” here means suffering, as in the “Passion” of Christ.) It has three layers. In the middle is Perpetua’s own diary, written in prison, in the first person, describing her arrest, her family, her visions and her trial, right up to the day before she died. Next to it is a shorter account of a dream written by Saturus, the man who had taught her the faith. Around both of them is a frame written by an editor, an unnamed Christian in Carthage who gathered the pieces together soon after the martyrs died, added an introduction, and described what happened in the arena, which Perpetua of course could not write herself. Some people have guessed that the editor was the famous Carthaginian writer Tertullian. Nobody knows for certain. Perpetua’s section is widely thought to be the oldest surviving piece of writing by a Christian woman. Of all the women who followed Jesus in the church’s first two centuries, the first whose own words we can still read was a young mother in a prison, writing in the weeks before her death. She ended her diary with a sentence that tells you she knew exactly what she was doing. This is what I did, she wrote, up to the day before the games; what happens at the games themselves, let someone else write, if they want to. Carthage, About the Year 200 Carthage stood on the coast of North Africa, close to where Tunis, in Tunisia, stands today. Once Rome’s great rival, it had been destroyed and rebuilt as a Roman city, and by Perpetua’s time it was one of the largest and richest cities in the western half of the empire, with a huge amphitheatre where crowds watched gladiators and wild animals. The church in Carthage was growing, and that made people nervous. Christians would not offer sacrifice to the gods of Rome or to the emperor’s well-being, and to many Romans that looked like disloyalty, even a danger to the city. Persecution in this period was not constant everywhere. It came in waves, often stirred up locally. Around 202 and 203, in the reign of the emperor Septimius Severus (who was himself born in North Africa), a wave broke over Carthage. A few years earlier, Tertullian, who lived in Carthage, had written a bold defence of the Christians addressed to the Roman authorities. Near the end of it he wrote the line he is most remembered for. In the usual English it is: “The blood of Christians is seed.” The more you kill us, he meant, the more of us there will be. Perpetua was about to show what it meant. Who She Was The editor tells us that Perpetua was “well born,” well educated, and married in the respectable way. Her father was alive, and so was her mother. She had two brothers, one of them, like her, a catechumen. She had an aunt she mentions once. Her husband is never mentioned at all, not by her and not by the editor. We do not know whether he had died, or left, or simply was not part of the story. It is one of the silences in the account, and it is better to leave it as a silence than to fill it with a guess. A catechumen was a person who was learning the Christian faith and preparing to be baptized. In the church of that time, preparation could last a long while, and people often waited months or years for baptism. So when Perpetua was arrested, she had not yet been baptized. She was a believer who had not yet gone through the water. She was not arrested alone. With her were several other young catechumens: two who were slaves, Revocatus and a young woman named Felicity, and two others, Saturninus and Secundulus. Felicity was pregnant, about eight months along. Their teacher, Saturus, was not with them when they were taken. Later, of his own free will, he went to the authorities and gave himself up so that he could share what was happening to the people he had taught. In Roman society a noblewoman and a pregnant slave would never have sat at the same table. In this account they are simply sisters, and they would die side by side. The Dark A few days after the scene with the pitcher, while the father was staying away, the catechumens were baptized. We are not told who baptized them or exactly where. Perpetua tells us only one thing about it: that as she came out of the water, she felt the Spirit prompting her to ask for nothing else from it except endurance in the body. She knew what was coming. Then they were put in prison, and Perpetua was terrified. She was honest about that. She had never known darkness like it, she wrote. It was crowded and stiflingly hot, and the soldiers pushed the prisoners around and squeezed them for bribes. On top of all of it, she was sick with worry for her baby. Two deacons of the church, whom she names as Tertius and Pomponius, paid the guards so that the prisoners could spend a few hours in a better part of the prison. There Perpetua nursed her son, who was weak with hunger. She talked with her mother and her brother, and handed the baby to them to look after. She saw how much they were suffering because of her, and she said it hurt her to see it. For several days she lived with that anxiety. Then she was given permission to keep the baby with her in the prison. And at once, she wrote, she grew strong again. Her worry for him lifted, and her prison suddenly became like a palace to her, so that she would rather be there than anywhere else. The Ladder Perpetua’s brother came to her with a request. You are greatly honoured now, he told her (this is her report of what he said, not a word-for-word record), so ask God for a vision, and find out whether this will end in suffering or in release. Perpetua had already found that she could speak with the Lord, and she promised him she would tell him the next day. She asked. And she saw this. There was a ladder, enormously tall, reaching all the way up to heaven. It was made of bronze, and it was so narrow that only one person could climb it at a time. Fixed to its sides were all kinds of iron weapons: swords, spears, hooks, knives. Anyone who climbed carelessly, without looking up, would be torn by them. And under the ladder lay a huge serpent, waiting to attack anyone who tried to climb and to frighten them off. Saturus went up first. At the top he turned and called down to her that he was waiting for her, and told her to be careful that the serpent did not bite her. She answered that in the name of Jesus Christ it would not hurt her. And then, she says, the serpent slowly put out its head from under the ladder, as if it were afraid of her, and she used its head as the first step, and climbed. At the top she saw a huge garden. In the middle of it sat a tall man with white hair, dressed as a shepherd, milking sheep. Around him stood many thousands of people dressed in white. He lifted his head, looked at her, and welcomed her as his child. He gave her a mouthful of the cheese he was making, and she took it in her cupped hands and ate it, and everyone standing round said “Amen.” At that sound she woke up, still tasting something sweet. She told her brother what she had seen. They both understood what it meant. It would not be release. From then on, she wrote, they stopped hoping in anything this world could give. Christians have long heard in the trodden serpent’s head an echo of the Bible’s first promise, that the woman’s offspring “will crush your head” (Genesis 3:15). Perpetua did not explain her dream that way herself. But she clearly understood who the shepherd was, who the serpent was, and which of them had already won. “Have Pity on My Grey Hair” A rumour went round that the prisoners were going to be given a hearing. Perpetua’s father came in from the city, worn out with grief, and tried one last time. This time he did not shout. Perpetua records what he said, and it is one of the most painful passages in the whole account. He begged her to have pity on his grey hair. He reminded her that he had raised her, that he had loved her more than her brothers. He asked her to think of her mother and her aunt and her brothers, and of her son, who would not be able to live after she was gone. He told her not to destroy them all. He kissed her hands and threw himself at her feet, weeping, and he no longer called her “daughter” but “lady,” the way a servant would address his mistress. Perpetua says she was grieved for him, because he was the only one of her whole family who would not be glad at what she was about to suffer. She tried to comfort him. Whatever happened at the trial, she told him, would be what God willed, because, in the old translation, “we are not placed in our own power, but in that of God.” He went away in deep sorrow. Perpetua was not cold. She grieved over her father on almost every page she wrote about him. But she would not stop being what she was to make the pain stop, even his pain. Jesus had said that anyone who loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:37). Very few people in history have had to live that verse as literally as Perpetua did. The Hearing One day, while they were eating, the prisoners were suddenly taken away to the forum, the public square, for their hearing. A huge crowd gathered. The judge was a Roman official named Hilarianus, who was acting governor of the province because the governor had recently died. One by one the others were questioned, and one by one they confessed that they were Christians. Then it was Perpetua’s turn. At that moment her father appeared, holding her baby son. He pulled her down off the step and begged her to offer the sacrifice and have pity on the child. Hilarianus joined in. Spare your father’s grey hair, he told her; spare your little boy; offer a sacrifice for the safety of the emperors. It was a small act, and many in the crowd must have thought her mad to refuse. She said she would not. He asked her plainly whether she was a Christian. And she said that she was. Her father kept trying to pull her down, and Hilarianus ordered him thrown to the ground and beaten with a rod. Perpetua wrote that she felt it as if she herself had been struck, and that she grieved for him in his miserable old age. Then Hilarianus sentenced them all to be thrown to the wild beasts in the arena. And Perpetua wrote that they went back down to the prison cheerful. There was one more sorrow. Her baby had been used to nursing and staying with her in the prison, and she sent the deacon Pomponius to her father to ask for him. Her father refused to give the child back. And then, she says, as God willed it, the baby no longer wanted to nurse, and she was not left in pain or fever. She did not have to be tormented, she wrote, either by worry for the child or by pain in her body. She saw even that as a mercy. The Last Days In the days that remained, Perpetua had more visions, two of them bringing her comfort about a little brother, Dinocrates, who had died of a disease at seven. The last came on the day before the games. She dreamed that she was led into the arena and fought not an animal but a frightening man, an Egyptian, and trod on his head, and a tall figure gave her a branch of victory and said, “Peace be with you, daughter.” She woke understanding that she would fight not with beasts but with the devil, and that the victory would be hers. A military officer in charge of the prison, named Pudens, began to treat the prisoners with respect, because he could see, the editor says, some great power in them. He let their friends visit. Saturus had his own dream, which the editor included in his words: he and Perpetua were carried by angels into a garden of light, where voices sang “Holy, holy, holy” without end. The editor also tells us about Felicity. She was by now eight months pregnant, and she was distressed, because Roman law did not allow a pregnant woman to be executed, and she was afraid she would be held back and later put to death among strangers instead of with her friends. Her companions prayed with her, three days before the games. Immediately afterwards her labour began, and she gave birth to a baby girl. It was a hard birth, and she cried out in pain. One of the prison guards mocked her: if this hurts you so much, what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts? Felicity’s reply has been remembered ever since. In the old translation: “I now suffer that which I suffer; but then there will be another in me, who will suffer for me, because I also am about to suffer for Him.” A Christian woman, one of the “sisters,” took the baby girl and raised her as her own daughter. Felicity was a slave. Nobody else in Carthage would have thought her words worth writing down. The church did. The Arena The editor’s account of the last day, 7 March 203, is honest, and we will be honest too, without lingering. The prisoners walked from the prison to the amphitheatre, the editor says, as if they were going to heaven, joyful, with calm faces. Perpetua walked steadily, her face shining, singing a psalm. When the officials tried to make them dress in costumes as priests and priestesses of the Roman gods, Perpetua refused: they had come of their own accord, she said, precisely so that they would not have to do such things. The officials gave way. The men faced leopards, a bear and a boar. Perpetua and Felicity were sent in against a wild cow, and both were knocked down and hurt. The account remembers small, human things about Perpetua in that moment: that she pulled her torn tunic straight to cover herself, that she asked for a pin to put up her hair, and that, seeing Felicity on the ground, she went over, gave her her hand, and helped her up. Afterwards, at the gate, she seemed to come out of a kind of daze and asked when they were going to be sent against the cow. She would not believe it had already happened until she saw the marks on her own body. Then she called over her brother and another catechumen and said to them, in the old translation: “Stand fast in the faith, and love one another, all of you, and be not offended at my sufferings.” At the end, the martyrs who were still alive exchanged the kiss of peace with one another, and were put to death by the sword. The editor records that the young gladiator sent to kill Perpetua was inexperienced and his hand shook, and that she herself guided it. Saturus, who had climbed the ladder first in her dream, had died just before her. He had told Pudens, the prison officer, to remember his faith and not to be troubled but strengthened by what he saw. The editor says that Pudens, by then, was a believer. What Came After Perpetua and Felicity were not forgotten. Within a few years their story was being read aloud in the churches of North Africa. A generation later, Cyprian became bishop of Carthage and, in 258, was himself martyred there, beheaded under another emperor. Two centuries after Perpetua, the great North African bishop Augustine preached sermons on the day of her and Felicity’s feast, and in another of his writings he reminded readers that, much as they loved the account, it was not Scripture. Their names are still read and honoured on 7 March by Christians in many traditions around the world. But the most important thing about Perpetua is not her fame. It is the jug. At twenty-two, not yet baptized, with a baby who needed her and a father whose heart she was breaking, she still could not make herself anything other than what she had become: a person who belonged to Jesus Christ, and who believed that he had already crushed the serpent’s head. In Their Own Words “We are not placed in our own power, but in that of God.” — Perpetua, to her father, in The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (203) Think It Through Perpetua answered her father with a clay jug: a thing can only be called what it is. What would it mean for you to be “called” a Christian in a place where that costs you something? Where is that hardest for you? Perpetua loved her father and grieved for him, yet would not do what he asked. How can a person stay loving towards family who oppose their faith, without giving way? A noblewoman and a slave died side by side, and the slave’s words were written down and remembered. What does that tell you about what the gospel did to the way these Christians saw one another? Perpetua was honest in her diary about being terrified in the dark prison, and about being relieved when her father stayed away. Does it help you to know that a martyr felt fear? Why might it matter that she did not hide it? Read More on Ochorus Perpetua and Felicity appear in Fox’s Book of Martyrs, in the chapter “The Ten Primitive Persecutions,” which tells the story briefly (its date, 205, differs a little from the one most historians give, 203). For the church in Carthage a generation later, read The Treatises of Cyprian, by the bishop who led that same church through another persecution and died for his faith in 258; his author page carries a full biography. Tertullian’s own writings are not yet in the library.

fields.title: The Uganda Martyrs: Singing on the Road to Namugongo
fields.body_html:
On the morning of 3 June 1886, at a place called Namugongo in the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, a large group of young men and boys was brought out to die. Many of them were teenagers. The youngest, Kizito, was about fourteen. They had been marched there a week earlier, many of them bound, and held while the executioners gathered firewood. Now the wood was ready.

They had been offered their lives. All they had to do was give up “praying,” the word the people of the royal court used for following the new faith that missionaries had brought. They would not.

The people who were there remembered something about them that they could not explain. They were not weeping. Many of them were praying. Some were singing. The executioners wrapped them in reed mats and laid them on the great fire. Not one of the men who had been sent to kill them could make them say they were not Christians.

Who were these boys? And why did their own king want them dead?

A Kingdom by the Lake

Buganda was a powerful and highly organized kingdom on the northern shores of Lake Victoria, the great lake of East Africa. It was ruled by a king called the kabaka, whose word was law. Around him was a large court of chiefs, officials and servants. Among the most important of these servants were the pages: boys and young men from families all over the kingdom, sent to serve in the royal household. Being a page was an honour and a path to power. Many future chiefs started out as pages. But a page belonged completely to the kabaka. His life was in the king’s hands.

In the 1870s the kabaka was Mutesa I, a clever and curious ruler who welcomed visitors from the outside world. Arab and Swahili traders from the East African coast had already brought Islam to his court. In 1875 the explorer Henry Morton Stanley visited, and afterwards he wrote a letter to an English newspaper appealing for missionaries to come to Buganda. Missionaries of the Church Missionary Society, an Anglican society from England, arrived in 1877. Among them, from 1878, was a Scottish engineer named Alexander Mackay, who set up a workshop and a printing press and began putting parts of the Bible into Luganda. In 1879 Catholic missionaries arrived too, the White Fathers from France, among them Father Siméon Lourdel, whom the Baganda called “Mapeera.”

So, very quickly, the court of Buganda had three religions competing in it: the traditional religion of the kingdom, Islam, and two kinds of Christianity whose missionaries did not get on well with each other. And it was the young people, above all the pages, who were most eager to learn. They crowded into the missions to learn to read. They copied out lessons and passed them round. Older Christian pages taught the younger ones, often in secret, at night, in the pages’ quarters at the palace. The faith spread from boy to boy, much faster than the missionaries could have spread it themselves.

It is worth saying that the new faith was not the first to cost young people their lives at that court. In the 1870s Mutesa had also turned against Muslim converts among his pages, and a number of them were killed. Uganda remembers them too. The kabakas of that time were not afraid of one religion in particular. They were afraid of anything that put another loyalty above their own.

A Young King

Mutesa died in October 1884. His son Mwanga became kabaka. Mwanga was himself very young, probably about eighteen, and at first he seemed friendly to the Christians. Several of the leading Christian pages had been his companions.

That did not last. Mwanga was unstable and easily frightened, and the men around him, especially his chief minister, the katikkiro, warned him that the Christians were dangerous. Europeans were pushing into East Africa from every side; Germans were taking land to the south. It did not seem foolish to the court to wonder whether the missionaries were the first sign of foreign conquest, and whether the young Christians, who now talked of another King, were still truly loyal.

There was another reason, and it must be said plainly. Mwanga demanded that some of his pages give themselves to him sexually. Christian pages refused. They would not let themselves be abused, and the older ones did what they could to protect the younger boys from him. To a king who believed that his pages belonged to him completely, that refusal was an unbearable defiance. It is one of the reasons his anger fell on them so hard.

The First Three

The first Christians to die under Mwanga were three Anglican boys, pupils of the Protestant mission: Yusufu Lugalama, Makko Kakumba and Nuwa Sserwanga. (Their names are spelled in different ways in different books; Lugalama is sometimes written Rugarama.) On 31 January 1885 they were seized and, on the king’s orders, put to death by burning, after being cruelly wounded. Yusufu was young, perhaps eleven or twelve; accounts differ on the exact ages of all three.

We do not have a reliable record of what they said. What the accounts agree on is that they died because they were Christians, and that they did not save themselves by giving up their faith.

The missionaries were horrified, and so were many at court. For a while there was quiet. But the king had shown what he was prepared to do.

“I Have Purchased the Road”

Later that year, news reached Mwanga that a party of Europeans was approaching Buganda from the east, through the neighbouring land of Busoga. It was led by James Hannington, the newly appointed Anglican bishop for East Africa. In Buganda there was a saying that the kingdom’s conquerors would come from the east, and the court was alarmed. Mwanga ordered that the travellers be stopped and killed.

In October 1885, in Busoga, Hannington was seized, held for several days, and then put to death along with most of the African porters who had come with him. According to the account later reported by survivors, among his last words was a message for the king: “Tell Mwanga I have purchased the road to Uganda with my blood.” Hannington was thirty-eight.

Joseph Mukasa

At the heart of the royal household stood a Catholic Christian named Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe. He was a trusted senior servant who had charge of the pages, and he was one of the most respected Christians at court. He had served Mwanga for years and was close to him. He had also done his best to keep the boys in his care away from the king’s demands.

When Mukasa heard that the king had ordered the bishop killed, he did something very dangerous. He went to Mwanga and told him that he had done wrong: that to kill a man who came in peace was a crime. He was already in trouble with the king’s advisers for protecting the pages, and now he had rebuked the kabaka himself.

On 15 November 1885 Mwanga had him put to death. Joseph Mukasa was beheaded, and his body was burned. He was about twenty-five. Witnesses later reported that before he died he sent the king a message: he had been condemned unjustly, he said, but he forgave Mwanga with all his heart. He is honoured as the first Catholic martyr of Uganda.

Charles Lwanga

That same night, Father Lourdel baptized a group of young men, among them a man named Charles Lwanga. Lwanga was in his twenties, a strong and steady young man from the household’s staff, and he now took up much of Mukasa’s role. He became the leader of the Christian pages in the royal audience hall, and he took on Mukasa’s work of protecting them, especially the youngest.

For six months he and the others lived under the threat. They knew that the king might strike again at any time. They kept praying, kept meeting, kept teaching one another. More boys asked to be baptized, and their teachers, both Catholic and Anglican, began to baptize them sooner, knowing there might not be much time.

Among the boys in Lwanga’s care was Kizito. He was about fourteen, cheerful, and the youngest of the group. He had wanted to be baptized for a long time, but he had been asked to wait, because of his age. Lwanga had kept a protective eye on him, and Kizito trusted him completely.

The Day of Choosing

In late May 1886, the storm broke. Mwanga came back to his lakeside palace at Munyonyo from a hunting trip. When he discovered that one of his young attendants, Denis Ssebuggwawo, had been teaching the Christian faith to another boy, he flew into a rage and attacked Denis with a spear. Denis was put to death that same night.

That night, 25 May, believing that the end had come, Charles Lwanga gathered the Catholic catechumens among the pages and baptized several of them himself. One was Kizito.

The next morning, 26 May 1886, Mwanga called his pages together and divided them. Those who did not pray, he told them in effect, should stand on one side, near him; those who prayed should go to the other side. The accounts disagree on his exact words, so we will not pretend to give them. But the meaning was plain to everyone. One side was life. The other side was death.

Charles Lwanga and Kizito walked across. So did many others, Catholic and Anglican. They did not do it in a group with their eyes shut, swept along. Each one crossed by himself.

Mwanga asked them whether they meant to keep praying. They said they did. He condemned them to death, and they were handed over to the chief executioner, Mukajanga, to be taken to Namugongo, the traditional place of execution, a long walk away. Some of the condemned were killed on the road. Gonzaga Gonza could not keep up because of his chains, and was put to death on the way. Matthias Kalemba Mulumba, an older chief who had long been a seeker after God, was taken away and killed separately near the capital. Over those days other Christians who were not pages were hunted down and killed in other places, among them Andrew Kaggwa, the leader of the royal drummers, and Noe Mawaggali.

At Namugongo the prisoners were kept for a week while the great pyre was built.

Namugongo

One of the condemned was Mbaga Tuzinde, a young page who was a son in the household of Mukajanga, the chief executioner himself. His family begged him to give up his faith, or at least to hide until the danger passed. He would not. In the end he was put to death separately, shortly before the others, killed with a blow before his body was burned.

Charles Lwanga was also taken aside and burned separately, on the morning of 3 June, a little before the rest. Catholic tradition, drawn from people who were there, remembers him speaking calmly to his executioner as he died and urging him to repent and believe. We do not have a record of his exact words that historians can be sure of, so we will leave them there.

Then the others were wrapped in mats of reeds and laid on the fire. Witnesses remembered that they prayed and sang. One account says that the dying called on the name of God and that the executioners were astonished that none of them begged for mercy. It was Ascension Day, the day when the church remembers Jesus rising into heaven.

How many died that day? The honest answer is that the sources differ. The Catholic Church counts thirteen of its own members burned at Namugongo on 3 June, with Charles Lwanga burned separately, and Anglican martyrs died there too. In all, more than two dozen people were killed at Namugongo that day, and some accounts give more, because not everyone who died was recorded by name, and some of those burned may not have been Christians at all but people caught up in the same purge. Across the whole persecution, from January 1885 to January 1887, the Catholic Church honours twenty-two martyrs by name and the Church of Uganda honours twenty-three Anglican martyrs; many historians think the total number of people killed was higher still.

Why would boys do this? It is the question the king himself could not answer. Some of them were very new believers. Most of them could read only a little, and they had only parts of the Bible in their own language. But they had understood enough. They had understood that Jesus was a King above every king, including the kabaka, and that he had died and risen for them. They believed that he had made them his own, and that death could not take them out of his hands. The words of Jesus that they had learned from their teachers were not complicated: “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). They simply believed them.

What Came After

The persecution did not destroy the church in Buganda. It did the opposite. Those who had seen the young men die did not forget how they died, and many began to ask what kind of faith could make boys sing on a fire. People went on learning in secret. Within a few years the political world of Buganda had turned upside down. In 1888 Mwanga was driven from his throne by an alliance of Christian and Muslim chiefs; there followed years of civil war, with Mwanga restored and then, in the end, exiled. In 1903 he died in exile in the Seychelles, having been baptized there as an Anglican Christian, an end very few would have predicted.

The church in Uganda grew with remarkable speed. The whole Bible was translated into Luganda, and Baganda Christians carried the gospel to other peoples across the region, often going where no foreign missionary had gone. Within a generation the faith was no longer a foreign mission but the church of a whole people. In the 1930s it would be the birthplace of the East African Revival, which spread across Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania and beyond. And Uganda’s Christians would be tested again. In 1977, Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered for standing up to the dictator Idi Amin, and Bishop Festo Kivengere had to flee the country.

In 1920 the Catholic martyrs were beatified, and in 1964 Pope Paul VI declared the twenty-two Catholic martyrs saints, among the first modern saints from sub-Saharan Africa. In 1969 he visited Uganda himself and prayed at Namugongo. Today there is a Catholic shrine and an Anglican shrine there, close to the place where the fires were lit. Every year on 3 June, Martyrs’ Day, a public holiday in Uganda, huge crowds of pilgrims, Catholic and Anglican, gather at Namugongo. Many of them walk there for days, from all over Uganda and from Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and further away. They come to remember boys who were no older than many of the pilgrims themselves.

Kizito was fourteen. He had been baptized for about a week.

In Their Own Words

“Tell Mwanga that he has condemned me unjustly, but I forgive him with all my heart.”

— Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe, message to the kabaka as reported by witnesses (1885)

Think It Through

  1. The Christian pages learned their faith mostly from one another: older boys teaching younger ones, often in secret. Who has passed the faith on to you, and who might you be passing it on to?
  2. The pages refused to let a powerful man abuse them, and the older ones protected the younger. What does their story say about the worth and dignity of every young person’s body and life, and about standing up for others who are vulnerable?
  3. On 26 May 1886 each page had to cross the floor alone. Faith can be shared in a group, but in the end each person decides for themselves. What does “crossing the floor” look like for a teenager today?
  4. Joseph Mukasa forgave the king who condemned him, and Mwanga himself was baptized years later. What does that say about how far God’s mercy can reach, and about whom we should pray for?
