fields.body_text: On the morning of 3 June 1886, at a place called Namugongo in the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, a large group of young men and boys was brought out to die. Many of them were teenagers. The youngest, Kizito, was about fourteen. They had been marched there a week earlier, many of them bound, and held while the executioners gathered firewood. Now the wood was ready. They had been offered their lives. All they had to do was give up “praying,” the word the people of the royal court used for following the new faith that missionaries had brought. They would not. The people who were there remembered something about them that they could not explain. They were not weeping. Many of them were praying. Some were singing. The executioners wrapped them in reed mats and laid them on the great fire. Not one of the men who had been sent to kill them could make them say they were not Christians. Who were these boys? And why did their own king want them dead? A Kingdom by the Lake Buganda was a powerful and highly organized kingdom on the northern shores of Lake Victoria, the great lake of East Africa. It was ruled by a king called the kabaka, whose word was law. Around him was a large court of chiefs, officials and servants. Among the most important of these servants were the pages: boys and young men from families all over the kingdom, sent to serve in the royal household. Being a page was an honour and a path to power. Many future chiefs started out as pages. But a page belonged completely to the kabaka. His life was in the king’s hands. In the 1870s the kabaka was Mutesa I, a clever and curious ruler who welcomed visitors from the outside world. Arab and Swahili traders from the East African coast had already brought Islam to his court. In 1875 the explorer Henry Morton Stanley visited, and afterwards he wrote a letter to an English newspaper appealing for missionaries to come to Buganda. Missionaries of the Church Missionary Society, an Anglican society from England, arrived in 1877. Among them, from 1878, was a Scottish engineer named Alexander Mackay, who set up a workshop and a printing press and began putting parts of the Bible into Luganda. In 1879 Catholic missionaries arrived too, the White Fathers from France, among them Father Siméon Lourdel, whom the Baganda called “Mapeera.” So, very quickly, the court of Buganda had three religions competing in it: the traditional religion of the kingdom, Islam, and two kinds of Christianity whose missionaries did not get on well with each other. And it was the young people, above all the pages, who were most eager to learn. They crowded into the missions to learn to read. They copied out lessons and passed them round. Older Christian pages taught the younger ones, often in secret, at night, in the pages’ quarters at the palace. The faith spread from boy to boy, much faster than the missionaries could have spread it themselves. It is worth saying that the new faith was not the first to cost young people their lives at that court. In the 1870s Mutesa had also turned against Muslim converts among his pages, and a number of them were killed. Uganda remembers them too. The kabakas of that time were not afraid of one religion in particular. They were afraid of anything that put another loyalty above their own. A Young King Mutesa died in October 1884. His son Mwanga became kabaka. Mwanga was himself very young, probably about eighteen, and at first he seemed friendly to the Christians. Several of the leading Christian pages had been his companions. That did not last. Mwanga was unstable and easily frightened, and the men around him, especially his chief minister, the katikkiro, warned him that the Christians were dangerous. Europeans were pushing into East Africa from every side; Germans were taking land to the south. It did not seem foolish to the court to wonder whether the missionaries were the first sign of foreign conquest, and whether the young Christians, who now talked of another King, were still truly loyal. There was another reason, and it must be said plainly. Mwanga demanded that some of his pages give themselves to him sexually. Christian pages refused. They would not let themselves be abused, and the older ones did what they could to protect the younger boys from him. To a king who believed that his pages belonged to him completely, that refusal was an unbearable defiance. It is one of the reasons his anger fell on them so hard. The First Three The first Christians to die under Mwanga were three Anglican boys, pupils of the Protestant mission: Yusufu Lugalama, Makko Kakumba and Nuwa Sserwanga. (Their names are spelled in different ways in different books; Lugalama is sometimes written Rugarama.) On 31 January 1885 they were seized and, on the king’s orders, put to death by burning, after being cruelly wounded. Yusufu was young, perhaps eleven or twelve; accounts differ on the exact ages of all three. We do not have a reliable record of what they said. What the accounts agree on is that they died because they were Christians, and that they did not save themselves by giving up their faith. The missionaries were horrified, and so were many at court. For a while there was quiet. But the king had shown what he was prepared to do. “I Have Purchased the Road” Later that year, news reached Mwanga that a party of Europeans was approaching Buganda from the east, through the neighbouring land of Busoga. It was led by James Hannington, the newly appointed Anglican bishop for East Africa. In Buganda there was a saying that the kingdom’s conquerors would come from the east, and the court was alarmed. Mwanga ordered that the travellers be stopped and killed. In October 1885, in Busoga, Hannington was seized, held for several days, and then put to death along with most of the African porters who had come with him. According to the account later reported by survivors, among his last words was a message for the king: “Tell Mwanga I have purchased the road to Uganda with my blood.” Hannington was thirty-eight. Joseph Mukasa At the heart of the royal household stood a Catholic Christian named Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe. He was a trusted senior servant who had charge of the pages, and he was one of the most respected Christians at court. He had served Mwanga for years and was close to him. He had also done his best to keep the boys in his care away from the king’s demands. When Mukasa heard that the king had ordered the bishop killed, he did something very dangerous. He went to Mwanga and told him that he had done wrong: that to kill a man who came in peace was a crime. He was already in trouble with the king’s advisers for protecting the pages, and now he had rebuked the kabaka himself. On 15 November 1885 Mwanga had him put to death. Joseph Mukasa was beheaded, and his body was burned. He was about twenty-five. Witnesses later reported that before he died he sent the king a message: he had been condemned unjustly, he said, but he forgave Mwanga with all his heart. He is honoured as the first Catholic martyr of Uganda. Charles Lwanga That same night, Father Lourdel baptized a group of young men, among them a man named Charles Lwanga. Lwanga was in his twenties, a strong and steady young man from the household’s staff, and he now took up much of Mukasa’s role. He became the leader of the Christian pages in the royal audience hall, and he took on Mukasa’s work of protecting them, especially the youngest. For six months he and the others lived under the threat. They knew that the king might strike again at any time. They kept praying, kept meeting, kept teaching one another. More boys asked to be baptized, and their teachers, both Catholic and Anglican, began to baptize them sooner, knowing there might not be much time. Among the boys in Lwanga’s care was Kizito. He was about fourteen, cheerful, and the youngest of the group. He had wanted to be baptized for a long time, but he had been asked to wait, because of his age. Lwanga had kept a protective eye on him, and Kizito trusted him completely. The Day of Choosing In late May 1886, the storm broke. Mwanga came back to his lakeside palace at Munyonyo from a hunting trip. When he discovered that one of his young attendants, Denis Ssebuggwawo, had been teaching the Christian faith to another boy, he flew into a rage and attacked Denis with a spear. Denis was put to death that same night. That night, 25 May, believing that the end had come, Charles Lwanga gathered the Catholic catechumens among the pages and baptized several of them himself. One was Kizito. The next morning, 26 May 1886, Mwanga called his pages together and divided them. Those who did not pray, he told them in effect, should stand on one side, near him; those who prayed should go to the other side. The accounts disagree on his exact words, so we will not pretend to give them. But the meaning was plain to everyone. One side was life. The other side was death. Charles Lwanga and Kizito walked across. So did many others, Catholic and Anglican. They did not do it in a group with their eyes shut, swept along. Each one crossed by himself. Mwanga asked them whether they meant to keep praying. They said they did. He condemned them to death, and they were handed over to the chief executioner, Mukajanga, to be taken to Namugongo, the traditional place of execution, a long walk away. Some of the condemned were killed on the road. Gonzaga Gonza could not keep up because of his chains, and was put to death on the way. Matthias Kalemba Mulumba, an older chief who had long been a seeker after God, was taken away and killed separately near the capital. Over those days other Christians who were not pages were hunted down and killed in other places, among them Andrew Kaggwa, the leader of the royal drummers, and Noe Mawaggali. At Namugongo the prisoners were kept for a week while the great pyre was built. Namugongo One of the condemned was Mbaga Tuzinde, a young page who was a son in the household of Mukajanga, the chief executioner himself. His family begged him to give up his faith, or at least to hide until the danger passed. He would not. In the end he was put to death separately, shortly before the others, killed with a blow before his body was burned. Charles Lwanga was also taken aside and burned separately, on the morning of 3 June, a little before the rest. Catholic tradition, drawn from people who were there, remembers him speaking calmly to his executioner as he died and urging him to repent and believe. We do not have a record of his exact words that historians can be sure of, so we will leave them there. Then the others were wrapped in mats of reeds and laid on the fire. Witnesses remembered that they prayed and sang. One account says that the dying called on the name of God and that the executioners were astonished that none of them begged for mercy. It was Ascension Day, the day when the church remembers Jesus rising into heaven. How many died that day? The honest answer is that the sources differ. The Catholic Church counts thirteen of its own members burned at Namugongo on 3 June, with Charles Lwanga burned separately, and Anglican martyrs died there too. In all, more than two dozen people were killed at Namugongo that day, and some accounts give more, because not everyone who died was recorded by name, and some of those burned may not have been Christians at all but people caught up in the same purge. Across the whole persecution, from January 1885 to January 1887, the Catholic Church honours twenty-two martyrs by name and the Church of Uganda honours twenty-three Anglican martyrs; many historians think the total number of people killed was higher still. Why would boys do this? It is the question the king himself could not answer. Some of them were very new believers. Most of them could read only a little, and they had only parts of the Bible in their own language. But they had understood enough. They had understood that Jesus was a King above every king, including the kabaka, and that he had died and risen for them. They believed that he had made them his own, and that death could not take them out of his hands. The words of Jesus that they had learned from their teachers were not complicated: “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). They simply believed them. What Came After The persecution did not destroy the church in Buganda. It did the opposite. Those who had seen the young men die did not forget how they died, and many began to ask what kind of faith could make boys sing on a fire. People went on learning in secret. Within a few years the political world of Buganda had turned upside down. In 1888 Mwanga was driven from his throne by an alliance of Christian and Muslim chiefs; there followed years of civil war, with Mwanga restored and then, in the end, exiled. In 1903 he died in exile in the Seychelles, having been baptized there as an Anglican Christian, an end very few would have predicted. The church in Uganda grew with remarkable speed. The whole Bible was translated into Luganda, and Baganda Christians carried the gospel to other peoples across the region, often going where no foreign missionary had gone. Within a generation the faith was no longer a foreign mission but the church of a whole people. In the 1930s it would be the birthplace of the East African Revival, which spread across Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania and beyond. And Uganda’s Christians would be tested again. In 1977, Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered for standing up to the dictator Idi Amin, and Bishop Festo Kivengere had to flee the country. In 1920 the Catholic martyrs were beatified, and in 1964 Pope Paul VI declared the twenty-two Catholic martyrs saints, among the first modern saints from sub-Saharan Africa. In 1969 he visited Uganda himself and prayed at Namugongo. Today there is a Catholic shrine and an Anglican shrine there, close to the place where the fires were lit. Every year on 3 June, Martyrs’ Day, a public holiday in Uganda, huge crowds of pilgrims, Catholic and Anglican, gather at Namugongo. Many of them walk there for days, from all over Uganda and from Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and further away. They come to remember boys who were no older than many of the pilgrims themselves. Kizito was fourteen. He had been baptized for about a week. fields.title: John Newton: The Storm That Would Not Let Him Go
fields.body_html:
In the dark early hours of 10 March 1748, a young English sailor woke in his hammock aboard a merchant ship called the Greyhound, somewhere in the North Atlantic, to the sound of the sea breaking over the deck and water pouring into the cabin below. Someone was shouting that the ship was sinking.

His name was John Newton. He was twenty-two years old, and by his own account he was one of the most foul-mouthed, God-mocking men on board. The crew had come to regard him as a kind of curse. He was famous among them for inventing new ways to blaspheme.

He scrambled for the ladder. On the way up, the captain called to him to fetch a knife, and while he went back for it, another man climbed up in his place. That man was swept overboard almost at once and was never seen again. Newton never forgot that someone else had stood where he should have been standing.

The storm had torn away part of the ship’s side. The Greyhound was an old vessel, and the sea was getting in faster than it could be thrown out. The men worked the pumps and bailed with buckets, hour after hour, in freezing spray. What kept the ship afloat, Newton later decided, was its cargo: beeswax and wood, lighter than water, packed in the hold.

At about nine in the morning, worn out, Newton went to speak to the captain. As he turned away, he heard himself say something he had not said seriously in years. In his own words, it came out “almost without any meaning”: “If this will not do, the Lord have mercy upon us!”

He stopped. Mercy? The words had come out of his own mouth, and they frightened him more than the sea did. If there really was a God, Newton thought, what mercy could there possibly be for a man like him?

A Mother’s Hymns

John Newton was born in Wapping, a crowded district of sailors and ships beside the River Thames in London, on 24 July 1725. His father, also called John, was the master of a merchant ship and was often away at sea for long stretches. His mother, Elizabeth, was a quiet, devout woman who belonged to a group of Christians outside the official Church of England, known then as Dissenters.

She poured her faith into her only son. She taught him to read before he was four. She taught him Bible passages, hymns and the short question-and-answer summaries of belief called catechisms. She hoped, he later wrote, that he would grow up to be a minister.

She was also ill with tuberculosis, which people then called consumption. In July 1732 she died. John was six, a couple of weeks short of his seventh birthday. Almost everything good he would later remember from his childhood belonged to the years before that summer.

His father married again, and John was sent away to a boarding school in Essex, where he was unhappy.

At Sea at Eleven

On his eleventh birthday, in 1736, John went to sea with his father. Over the next few years he made several voyages with his father to the Mediterranean, learning the ropes, the rigging and the rough language of the ship.

What is striking about the teenage John Newton is how many times he tried to be religious, and how many times it fell apart. In his Authentic Narrative, the account of his early life he published in 1764, he describes going through phase after phase of trying hard. Several times, after a scare or a narrow escape, he became very serious. He prayed, read the Bible, fasted, kept long lists of rules, and stopped swearing. Then, after a while, it all slipped away, and he went back to how he had been, usually worse.

Fear made a poor foundation. He described his religion in those years as a matter of keeping rules in order to earn God’s approval, and he never found any peace in it.

When he was about sixteen, he came across a book by the Earl of Shaftesbury, an English writer who argued that a person could be good and wise without needing the Christianity of the Bible. Newton read it eagerly. It made faith seem small and unnecessary. Not long afterwards, a sailor he admired, a man who openly rejected Christianity, finished the job. Newton stopped believing altogether. Worse, he became a missionary for unbelief: he enjoyed taking apart other people’s faith, and he mocked anyone who prayed.

Around the end of 1742 something else happened that would shape the rest of his life. His father had arranged a good job for him on a plantation in Jamaica. Before he sailed, John went to visit a family in Kent named Catlett, old friends of his mother. There he met their daughter Mary, whom everyone called Polly. She was about fourteen. He was seventeen and fell completely in love. He stayed with the Catletts so long that he missed his ship. The job in Jamaica went to someone else.

Pressed into the Navy

Britain was at war, and the Royal Navy needed men. In those days the navy used “press gangs”: groups of sailors with the legal right to seize able-bodied men, especially men with sea experience, and force them to serve on warships. In 1743, when he was eighteen, John Newton was caught by a press gang and taken aboard a warship, HMS Harwich.

His father used his connections to have him made a midshipman, a junior officer in training, which was far better than being an ordinary seaman. But John was miserable. The Harwich was due to sail for the East Indies, which meant being away for years, and he could not bear the thought of leaving Polly for so long. When the ship was at Plymouth, he was sent ashore on duty with a boat, and he ran.

He did not get far. Soldiers caught him on the road, a day or so later, and brought him back to the ship in chains. Deserting the navy was a serious crime. He was stripped and flogged in front of the whole ship’s company and demoted from midshipman to the lowest rank of seaman. The other officers were told not to speak to him. From being a young gentleman on his way up, he had become the ship’s lowest, most despised hand.

He later admitted that in the weeks that followed, his mind went to very dark places: he thought about taking revenge on the captain, and about throwing himself into the sea. He said that only a lingering love for Polly held him back. He was a lonely, furious teenager with no one to talk to, and he came closer to the edge than anyone around him knew.

Traded Away

When the Harwich reached the island of Madeira, in the Atlantic, in 1745, a merchant ship was in the harbour, bound for the coast of West Africa to trade. Newton managed to be exchanged onto it. He was glad to be free of the navy. He had no idea what he was going into.

The ship was in the slave trade. For about three hundred years, European and American traders bought African men, women and children, many of them captured in wars and raids, and carried them across the Atlantic in chained, overcrowded ships to be sold as slaves in the Americas. Huge numbers died on the way. It was one of the greatest crimes in human history, and in the 1740s it was a normal, legal and highly profitable business in Britain.

Newton was not troubled by it at all. On board his new ship he went on mocking God and the captain. When the ship reached the coast, he left it to work for a white slave trader who lived on the Plantain Islands, small islands off the coast of Sierra Leone, on the western bulge of Africa.

A Servant of Slaves

What happened next was the lowest point of his life, and he later told it without self-pity.

Soon after he arrived, he fell seriously ill with fever. His employer went away on a trading trip and left him in the care of the trader’s African partner, a powerful woman in the local trade. For reasons Newton never fully understood, she took a strong dislike to him. Sick and weak, he lay on a mat with almost nothing to eat. He remembered being so hungry that he went out at night to pull up roots from the ground and eat them raw. People mocked him; some threw limes at him as he lay helpless. Sometimes, he remembered, the only kindness he received came from Africans who were themselves in chains, who secretly passed him a little of their own tiny rations.

When his employer came back, he believed accusations that Newton had been stealing from him. After that, when they went out by boat, Newton was locked on the deck with a pint of rice for the day, in the open air through days of sun and nights of pouring rain, with almost no clothes. “I was locked upon deck,” he wrote, “with a pint of rice for my day’s allowance.” He began to look, he said, like a man in a state of misery that would have frightened anyone who had known him at home.

For about a year, the young man who would one day captain slave ships was treated almost as a slave himself. He later called himself, in the epitaph he wrote for his own grave, “a servant of slaves in Africa.” It is important to be clear about what this was and was not. He was not bought and sold, chained in a ship’s hold and carried across an ocean, as millions of Africans were. But he had a taste of hunger, contempt and helplessness, and he never forgot it.

There is one odd, stubborn detail from those months. Newton had brought with him a copy of Euclid, the ancient Greek textbook of geometry. In his worst days on the islands, he would take it to a remote part of the beach and work through the proofs by drawing the diagrams in the sand with a stick. Something in him refused to give up entirely.

Eventually he was allowed to go to work for another trader on the mainland, who treated him well. He began, for the first time in years, to do well for himself. He was even starting to like the life. He wrote home to his father, and his father asked the captains of ships trading on that coast to look out for his son.

The Greyhound

Early in 1747, a ship called the Greyhound passed along the coast where Newton was working. It was trading not in human beings but in gold, ivory, beeswax and a red dyewood. A trader on shore happened to send up a column of smoke as a signal, and the ship stopped. The captain asked whether anyone knew of a young man named John Newton. He had nearly missed him; Newton reckoned that if he had been a little further along the coast that day, the ship would have sailed past.

Newton did not want to go home. He had found a life he liked. The captain, by Newton’s own account, persuaded him partly by inventing a story about an inheritance waiting for him in England. But it was the thought of Polly, more than anything, that made him step into the boat.

The Greyhound spent another year trading on the African coast before setting out for England. Newton had nothing to do on board but wait, and he spent the time drinking, swearing and trying to talk the other sailors out of what little faith they had. Once, drunk, he nearly went over the side of the ship after his own hat. The captain told him more than once that he was a “Jonah,” the bringer of bad luck to a ship.

On 9 March 1748, the day before the storm, out of sheer boredom, he picked up a book from the ship’s small collection. It was The Imitation of Christ, a famous old book of Christian devotion by Thomas à Kempis. As he read, a question crept into his mind that he did not want: what if these things are true? He shut the book, and the thought, and went to bed. A few hours later the sea came through the side of the ship.

“Mercy! What Mercy?”

After he heard himself cry out for mercy that morning, Newton went back to the pumps. At noon he was sent to take the helm, steering the battered ship, and he stayed there until midnight. For hours, with nothing to do but hold the wheel, he thought about his life.

What he felt was not comfort. It was terror. All the Scripture he had learned at his mother’s side came back to him, and the verses that came back were warnings. He thought about what he had done: the people he had led away from faith, the God he had mocked. He thought there was no possibility he could be forgiven. But he also thought: if the Bible is true, then Jesus is real, and if Jesus is real, then perhaps.

The storm passed, but the danger did not. The ship had lost most of its food and was drifting, damaged, far off course. For four weeks the crew lived on a shrinking store of salted fish. Then the food ran out almost entirely. Newton started to read the New Testament seriously, for the first time since he was a boy. One verse, in the King James wording he read, gave him hope: “If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luke 11:13). He did not feel he had faith. But he could ask. So he asked.

On 8 April 1748, the Greyhound finally limped into Lough Swilly, a long sea inlet in the north of Ireland. Newton later noted that almost as soon as they anchored, a violent gale blew up. Had they still been at sea, they would have been lost. In the nearby town of Londonderry he went to church twice a day. He kept 10 March as a kind of second birthday for the rest of his life.

Not Yet Seeing

Here is the part of the story that many retellings leave out, and that Newton himself, to his credit, refused to leave out.

The storm did not turn him into the man who wrote “Amazing Grace.” Newton always said that his conversion was slow, not sudden. He wrote that he could not consider himself to have been a true believer, in the full sense of the word, until a considerable time after the storm. He stopped swearing and he started praying. But he went straight back to sea, and the trade he went back to was the slave trade.

In 1748 he sailed as first mate on a slave ship to the African coast. In 1750 he married Polly Catlett, and that same year he became captain of a slave ship, the Duke of Argyle. Later he commanded another, the African. On those voyages, hundreds of enslaved Africans were held in chains below his deck while Newton led his crew in prayers on Sunday above it. He wrote hymns of thanks to God in his cabin. He did not see any contradiction. Years later he admitted that at the time he had felt no scruple at all about the work. He thought of it as a respectable job, which most of his society thought it was.

That is hard to read, and it should be. It shows that a person can truly begin to turn to God and still be blind to a great evil in front of their eyes, especially an evil that everyone around them thinks is normal. Newton’s eyes were opened, but slowly, and too slowly for the people chained below his deck.

In 1754 a sudden seizure, a kind of fit, ended his career at sea. He took a job as a customs officer, a “tide surveyor,” in the port of Liverpool. In the evenings he taught himself Greek and Hebrew so he could read the Bible in its original languages. He went to hear the great preachers of the day, including George Whitefield. Slowly his faith deepened and settled. It had stopped being about keeping rules to earn God’s favour. He had come to see that his only hope was what Jesus had done for him, not what he did for Jesus.

What Came After

After several refusals, Newton was ordained as a clergyman in the Church of England in 1764 and sent to the small town of Olney in Buckinghamshire. The same year, he published his Authentic Narrative, which made him famous.

At Olney he became a close friend of the poet William Cowper, who struggled all his life with deep depression, and the two of them wrote hymns for their congregation. For a New Year’s Day service on 1 January 1773, Newton wrote a hymn to go with his sermon on 1 Chronicles 17, where King David says in wonder, “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?” The hymn began, “Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me!” It was published in Olney Hymns in 1779. Newton was not reaching for a dramatic word when he wrote “wretch.” He knew exactly what he meant by it.

In 1780 he moved to London to be rector of St Mary Woolnoth, a church in the City. In 1785 a young member of Parliament named William Wilberforce, who had recently come to faith, came to him for advice. Wilberforce was thinking of leaving politics. Newton urged him to stay, believing God could use him there. Wilberforce went on to lead the long campaign in Parliament against the slave trade.

In 1788, more than thirty years after he left the sea, Newton published Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade, an eyewitness account of the trade’s cruelty and a public confession of his own part in it. “It will always be a subject of humiliating reflection to me,” he wrote, “that I was once an active instrument in a business at which my heart now shudders.” That same year he gave evidence about the trade to a government committee. fields.body_text: In the dark early hours of 10 March 1748, a young English sailor woke in his hammock aboard a merchant ship called the Greyhound, somewhere in the North Atlantic, to the sound of the sea breaking over the deck and water pouring into the cabin below. Someone was shouting that the ship was sinking. His name was John Newton. He was twenty-two years old, and by his own account he was one of the most foul-mouthed, God-mocking men on board. The crew had come to regard him as a kind of curse. He was famous among them for inventing new ways to blaspheme. He scrambled for the ladder. On the way up, the captain called to him to fetch a knife, and while he went back for it, another man climbed up in his place. That man was swept overboard almost at once and was never seen again. Newton never forgot that someone else had stood where he should have been standing. The storm had torn away part of the ship’s side. The Greyhound was an old vessel, and the sea was getting in faster than it could be thrown out. The men worked the pumps and bailed with buckets, hour after hour, in freezing spray. What kept the ship afloat, Newton later decided, was its cargo: beeswax and wood, lighter than water, packed in the hold. At about nine in the morning, worn out, Newton went to speak to the captain. As he turned away, he heard himself say something he had not said seriously in years. In his own words, it came out “almost without any meaning”: “If this will not do, the Lord have mercy upon us!” He stopped. Mercy? The words had come out of his own mouth, and they frightened him more than the sea did. If there really was a God, Newton thought, what mercy could there possibly be for a man like him? A Mother’s Hymns John Newton was born in Wapping, a crowded district of sailors and ships beside the River Thames in London, on 24 July 1725. His father, also called John, was the master of a merchant ship and was often away at sea for long stretches. His mother, Elizabeth, was a quiet, devout woman who belonged to a group of Christians outside the official Church of England, known then as Dissenters. She poured her faith into her only son. She taught him to read before he was four. She taught him Bible passages, hymns and the short question-and-answer summaries of belief called catechisms. She hoped, he later wrote, that he would grow up to be a minister. She was also ill with tuberculosis, which people then called consumption. In July 1732 she died. John was six, a couple of weeks short of his seventh birthday. Almost everything good he would later remember from his childhood belonged to the years before that summer. His father married again, and John was sent away to a boarding school in Essex, where he was unhappy. At Sea at Eleven On his eleventh birthday, in 1736, John went to sea with his father. Over the next few years he made several voyages with his father to the Mediterranean, learning the ropes, the rigging and the rough language of the ship. What is striking about the teenage John Newton is how many times he tried to be religious, and how many times it fell apart. In his Authentic Narrative, the account of his early life he published in 1764, he describes going through phase after phase of trying hard. Several times, after a scare or a narrow escape, he became very serious. He prayed, read the Bible, fasted, kept long lists of rules, and stopped swearing. Then, after a while, it all slipped away, and he went back to how he had been, usually worse. Fear made a poor foundation. He described his religion in those years as a matter of keeping rules in order to earn God’s approval, and he never found any peace in it. When he was about sixteen, he came across a book by the Earl of Shaftesbury, an English writer who argued that a person could be good and wise without needing the Christianity of the Bible. Newton read it eagerly. It made faith seem small and unnecessary. Not long afterwards, a sailor he admired, a man who openly rejected Christianity, finished the job. Newton stopped believing altogether. Worse, he became a missionary for unbelief: he enjoyed taking apart other people’s faith, and he mocked anyone who prayed. Around the end of 1742 something else happened that would shape the rest of his life. His father had arranged a good job for him on a plantation in Jamaica. Before he sailed, John went to visit a family in Kent named Catlett, old friends of his mother. There he met their daughter Mary, whom everyone called Polly. She was about fourteen. He was seventeen and fell completely in love. He stayed with the Catletts so long that he missed his ship. The job in Jamaica went to someone else. Pressed into the Navy Britain was at war, and the Royal Navy needed men. In those days the navy used “press gangs”: groups of sailors with the legal right to seize able-bodied men, especially men with sea experience, and force them to serve on warships. In 1743, when he was eighteen, John Newton was caught by a press gang and taken aboard a warship, HMS Harwich. His father used his connections to have him made a midshipman, a junior officer in training, which was far better than being an ordinary seaman. But John was miserable. The Harwich was due to sail for the East Indies, which meant being away for years, and he could not bear the thought of leaving Polly for so long. When the ship was at Plymouth, he was sent ashore on duty with a boat, and he ran. He did not get far. Soldiers caught him on the road, a day or so later, and brought him back to the ship in chains. Deserting the navy was a serious crime. He was stripped and flogged in front of the whole ship’s company and demoted from midshipman to the lowest rank of seaman. The other officers were told not to speak to him. From being a young gentleman on his way up, he had become the ship’s lowest, most despised hand. He later admitted that in the weeks that followed, his mind went to very dark places: he thought about taking revenge on the captain, and about throwing himself into the sea. He said that only a lingering love for Polly held him back. He was a lonely, furious teenager with no one to talk to, and he came closer to the edge than anyone around him knew. Traded Away When the Harwich reached the island of Madeira, in the Atlantic, in 1745, a merchant ship was in the harbour, bound for the coast of West Africa to trade. Newton managed to be exchanged onto it. He was glad to be free of the navy. He had no idea what he was going into. The ship was in the slave trade. For about three hundred years, European and American traders bought African men, women and children, many of them captured in wars and raids, and carried them across the Atlantic in chained, overcrowded ships to be sold as slaves in the Americas. Huge numbers died on the way. It was one of the greatest crimes in human history, and in the 1740s it was a normal, legal and highly profitable business in Britain. Newton was not troubled by it at all. On board his new ship he went on mocking God and the captain. When the ship reached the coast, he left it to work for a white slave trader who lived on the Plantain Islands, small islands off the coast of Sierra Leone, on the western bulge of Africa. A Servant of Slaves What happened next was the lowest point of his life, and he later told it without self-pity. Soon after he arrived, he fell seriously ill with fever. His employer went away on a trading trip and left him in the care of the trader’s African partner, a powerful woman in the local trade. For reasons Newton never fully understood, she took a strong dislike to him. Sick and weak, he lay on a mat with almost nothing to eat. He remembered being so hungry that he went out at night to pull up roots from the ground and eat them raw. People mocked him; some threw limes at him as he lay helpless. He later called himself, in the epitaph he wrote for his own grave, “a servant of slaves in Africa.” It is important to be clear about what this was and was not. He was not bought and sold, chained in a ship’s hold and carried across an ocean, as millions of Africans were. But he had a taste of hunger, contempt and helplessness, and he never forgot it. There is one odd, stubborn detail from those months. Newton had brought with him a copy of Euclid, the ancient Greek textbook of geometry. In his worst days on the islands, he would take it to a remote part of the beach and work through the proofs by drawing the diagrams in the sand with a stick. Something in him refused to give up entirely. Eventually he was allowed to go to work for another trader on the mainland, who treated him well. He began, for the first time in years, to do well for himself. He was even starting to like the life. He wrote home to his father, and his father asked the captains of ships trading on that coast to look out for his son. The Greyhound Early in 1747, a ship called the Greyhound passed along the coast where Newton was working. It was trading not in human beings but in gold, ivory, beeswax and a red dyewood. A trader on shore happened to send up a column of smoke as a signal, and the ship stopped. The captain asked whether anyone knew of a young man named John Newton. He had nearly missed him; Newton reckoned that if he had been a little further along the coast that day, the ship would have sailed past. Newton did not want to go home. He had found a life he liked. The captain, by Newton’s own account, persuaded him partly by inventing a story about an inheritance waiting for him in England. But it was the thought of Polly, more than anything, that made him step into the boat. The Greyhound spent another year trading on the African coast before setting out for England. Newton had nothing to do on board but wait, and he spent the time drinking, swearing and trying to talk the other sailors out of what little faith they had. Once, drunk, he nearly went over the side of the ship after his own hat. The captain told him more than once that he was a “Jonah,” the bringer of bad luck to a ship. On 9 March 1748, the day before the storm, out of sheer boredom, he picked up a book from the ship’s small collection. It was The Imitation of Christ, a famous old book of Christian devotion by Thomas à Kempis. As he read, a question crept into his mind that he did not want: what if these things are true? He shut the book, and the thought, and went to bed. A few hours later the sea came through the side of the ship. “Mercy! What Mercy?” After he heard himself cry out for mercy that morning, Newton went back to the pumps. At noon he was sent to take the helm, steering the battered ship, and he stayed there until midnight. For hours, with nothing to do but hold the wheel, he thought about his life. What he felt was not comfort. It was terror. All the Scripture he had learned at his mother’s side came back to him, and the verses that came back were warnings. He thought about what he had done: the people he had led away from faith, the God he had mocked. He thought there was no possibility he could be forgiven. But he also thought: if the Bible is true, then Jesus is real, and if Jesus is real, then perhaps. The storm passed, but the danger did not. The ship had lost most of its food and was drifting, damaged, far off course. For four weeks the crew lived on a shrinking store of salted fish. Then the food ran out almost entirely. Newton started to read the New Testament seriously, for the first time since he was a boy. One verse, in the King James wording he read, gave him hope: “If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luke 11:13). He did not feel he had faith. But he could ask. So he asked. On 8 April 1748, the Greyhound finally limped into Lough Swilly, a long sea inlet in the north of Ireland. Newton later noted that almost as soon as they anchored, a violent gale blew up. Had they still been at sea, they would have been lost. In the nearby town of Londonderry he went to church twice a day. He kept 10 March as a kind of second birthday for the rest of his life. Not Yet Seeing Here is the part of the story that many retellings leave out, and that Newton himself, to his credit, refused to leave out. The storm did not turn him into the man who wrote “Amazing Grace.” Newton always said that his conversion was slow, not sudden. He wrote that he could not consider himself to have been a true believer, in the full sense of the word, until a considerable time after the storm. He stopped swearing and he started praying. But he went straight back to sea, and the trade he went back to was the slave trade. In 1748 he sailed as first mate on a slave ship to the African coast. In 1750 he married Polly Catlett, and that same year he became captain of a slave ship, the Duke of Argyle. Later he commanded another, the African. On those voyages, hundreds of enslaved Africans were held in chains below his deck while Newton led his crew in prayers on Sunday above it. He wrote hymns of thanks to God in his cabin. He did not see any contradiction. Years later he admitted that at the time he had felt no scruple at all about the work. He thought of it as a respectable job, which most of his society thought it was. That is hard to read, and it should be. It shows that a person can truly begin to turn to God and still be blind to a great evil in front of their eyes, especially an evil that everyone around them thinks is normal. Newton’s eyes were opened, but slowly, and too slowly for the people chained below his deck. In 1754 a sudden seizure, a kind of fit, ended his career at sea. He took a job as a customs officer, a “tide surveyor,” in the port of Liverpool. In the evenings he taught himself Greek and Hebrew so he could read the Bible in its original languages. He went to hear the great preachers of the day, including George Whitefield. Slowly his faith deepened and settled. It had stopped being about keeping rules to earn God’s favour. He had come to see that his only hope was what Jesus had done for him, not what he did for Jesus. What Came After After several refusals, Newton was ordained as a clergyman in the Church of England in 1764 and sent to the small town of Olney in Buckinghamshire. The same year, he published his Authentic Narrative, which made him famous. At Olney he became a close friend of the poet William Cowper, who struggled all his life with deep depression, and the two of them wrote hymns for their congregation. For a New Year’s Day service on 1 January 1773, Newton wrote a hymn to go with his sermon on 1 Chronicles 17, where King David says in wonder, “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?” The hymn began, “Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me!” It was published in Olney Hymns in 1779. fields.title: Sadhu Sundar Singh: The Boy Who Waited for the Train
fields.body_html:
At three o’clock on a cold December morning in 1904, in a village called Rampur in the Punjab, in the north of India, a fifteen-year-old boy got out of bed while the rest of the house was asleep. He went and poured cold water over himself, a ritual bath, the way a devout person in his family’s tradition prepared to pray. Then he went back to his room and began to pray.

His name was Sundar Singh. He was clever, proud and the son of a wealthy family, and for more than a year he had been desperately unhappy. He had decided that this would be his last night alive.

Not far from his house ran a railway line, and a train passed at five o’clock in the morning. He had made up his mind: if God did not show himself to him before then, he would go out and lay his head on the rails. He prayed, as he later remembered it, something like this: “O God, if there is a God, wilt thou show me the right way or I will kill myself.”

He prayed, and nothing happened. He kept praying. Four o’clock came. Then the minutes went by toward half past four, and the five o’clock train.

What happened next, Sundar told for the rest of his life, in India and in Europe and in America, without much change. The room filled with a light. In the light he saw a figure, and he knew who it was. It was Jesus, the one whose book he had burned three days before.

A Seeker in a Sikh Home

Sundar Singh was born on 3 September 1889 in Rampur, in what was then the Sikh-ruled state of Patiala. The Sikh religion had begun in the Punjab about four hundred years earlier with a teacher called Guru Nanak. Sikhs worship one God and follow the teachings of their Gurus, gathered in a holy book called the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh men traditionally leave their hair uncut and wear a turban, and the name Singh, which means “lion,” is shared by Sikh men.

His father, Sher Singh, was a landowner, wealthy and well connected. Sundar was the youngest son, and he grew up surrounded by comfort: servants, good food, fine clothes. But his home was open to more than one religious tradition. Holy men of different faiths came and went. Sundar learned the Sikh scriptures, and he also learned the Hindu ones. His biographers were told that by the age of seven he knew much of the Bhagavad Gita, one of the best-loved Hindu holy books, by heart.

The great influence of his childhood was his mother. She was deeply devout. She took him to visit sadhus, the wandering holy men of India who give up home, money and comfort to seek God, and she told him that one day he too should seek God like that, and find the peace that only God could give. Years later, when someone suggested that Sundar should go to a theological college, he said he had already been to the best one there was: his mother’s lap.

Fourteen and Angry

In 1903, when Sundar was fourteen, his mother died. An older brother died at around the same time.

It is hard to overstate what her death did to him. She had been the one who understood his questions. Now she was gone, and the questions remained, sharper than ever. He threw himself into religion with ferocious energy. He read the scriptures of his tradition, and of others. He tried the disciplines of yoga under a Hindu teacher, hoping for the inner stillness it promised. He kept every ceremony. And he found, as he put it later, no peace at all.

He was also attending a school in Rampur run by American Presbyterian missionaries. It was the best school available, and many Sikh and Hindu families sent their sons there. Every day the boys read from the Bible. Sundar hated it. To him, the Christian book was a foreign religion brought by foreigners. India was then ruled by Britain, and Christianity looked like the religion of the people in charge. Its claims seemed an insult to his mother’s faith and to the pride of a Sikh family.

So he fought it. He argued with the teachers. He later said that he threw stones at Christian preachers in the streets, and encouraged others to do the same. But there was a strange thing underneath the anger. He was not fighting a religion he did not care about. He was a boy who wanted peace with God more than anything, and he was furious with a book that claimed to offer it.

The Fire

In December 1904, when he was fifteen, Sundar did something that shocked even the people who agreed with him. “In the presence of my father,” he said later, “I cut up the Bible and other Christian books and put kerosene oil upon them and burnt them.”

Burning a holy book is a terrible insult in almost any religious tradition, including his own. His father, who did not want his son to become a Christian, still told him he should not have done it. Sundar did not care. He felt he had done something brave for the religion of his family.

But the fire did not make him feel better. If anything, it made it worse. He had burned the book, but not the questions. Three days later, he got up at three in the morning, poured cold water over himself, and began to pray his desperate prayer.

Before the Five O’Clock Train

Before we go on, a word to anyone reading this who has ever felt the way Sundar felt that night: that nothing makes sense, that there is no way out, that maybe it would be better not to be here. If you feel that way, or have felt it lately, please do not keep it to yourself. Tell an adult you trust today: a parent, a teacher, a youth leader, a school counsellor, a doctor. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number or a crisis line where you live. Sundar was alone with his despair that night, and it nearly killed him. You do not have to be alone with yours. Telling someone is not weakness. It is often the bravest thing a person can do.

Sundar told the story of what happened in the early morning many times, and the details stayed remarkably consistent. At about half past four, he said, the room filled with a bright light. At first he thought the house was on fire. Then he saw in the light the figure of a man, and the man’s face had, in Sundar’s words, “such an appearance of glory and love.” He had expected, if anyone appeared, that it might be the Buddha, or Krishna, or one of the holy figures of the traditions he knew. He had not expected Jesus.

He heard a voice speak to him in Hindustani, his own language. As Sundar remembered the words, the voice said: “How long will you persecute me? I have come to save you; you were praying to know the right way. Why do you not take it?”

If those words sound familiar, it may be because they echo another story. In the book of Acts, a young man named Saul, who was hunting down the first Christians, was stopped on the road to Damascus by a light from heaven and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (Acts 9:4). Sundar, like Saul, had been fighting the very one who was now calling him.

What struck Sundar most was not the light but the realisation that came with it. “The thought then came to me,” he said, “‘Jesus Christ is not dead but living and it must be He Himself.’” He had thought of Jesus as a teacher from long ago, someone in a book, the founder of the foreigners’ religion. Now he was convinced that Jesus was alive, and that the living Jesus had come to find him in his worst hour, three days after he had burned his words. “So I fell at His feet,” he said, “and got this wonderful Peace which I could not get anywhere else.”

The vision faded. The peace, he said, did not. The five o’clock train went by, and Sundar Singh did not go out to meet it.

It is fair to say that nobody else saw what Sundar saw that morning, and people who do not share his faith have explained it in other ways. What we can say is what he himself reported, and that it turned his life around completely and permanently.

Cast Out

He went straight to his father and woke him to say that he had become a Christian. His father, not unreasonably, told him he must be out of his mind; only three days earlier he had burned the Bible. Sundar’s answer, as he later remembered it, was that he had discovered Jesus Christ was alive and that he had decided to follow him.

His family did everything they could to change his mind. To them his decision was not just a private matter of belief. It brought shame on the family’s name and seemed to reject everything his mother had stood for. They reasoned with him. They offered him wealth and position. An uncle, according to his early biographers, showed him a great store of money and jewels and offered it all if he would give up this new faith. He refused. He cut off his long hair, the outward mark of a Sikh, which to his family was a final and painful sign that he meant it.

In the end his father disowned him and sent him away. Sundar’s early biographers record that before he left, he was given a last meal at home, and that poison had been mixed into his food. He became seriously ill on his way and reached a Christian household where he was cared for until he recovered. We cannot know every detail of this; it comes from his own account and from people close to him. But that he was driven out by the family that had loved him, and that he believed they had tried to kill him rather than see him become a Christian, is part of his story as he always told it.

He spent his first night as an outcast in the cold, under a tree, with no home, no family and no money. He later called it his first night in heaven. He had lost everything his family could give him, but he had found the peace that all that comfort had never given him.

On 3 September 1905, his sixteenth birthday, he was baptized in the Church of England in Simla, a town in the Himalayan foothills where the British government spent its summers.

The Saffron Robe

Only weeks after his baptism, Sundar made a choice that would shape the rest of his life. He put on the saffron-yellow robe of a sadhu, the Indian holy man who gives up everything to seek God. But he would be a sadhu with a difference: a sadhu who had found the One he sought, and who walked the roads to tell people about Jesus.

It was a deliberate choice. Most Christian preachers in India at the time were foreign missionaries or Indians who dressed and lived in a Western way. Sundar believed that Christ was not a foreigner, and that Indians should be able to see that the Christian faith could be lived in an Indian way. As a sadhu he owned almost nothing: a robe, a blanket and a New Testament. He took no money, ate what people gave him, and slept wherever he found himself, in caves, under trees, in the homes of strangers. He walked barefoot across the Punjab, into Kashmir, and further north and west. He was sixteen.

The robe opened doors, because many Indians honoured holy men. It also brought danger, because once people discovered whom this sadhu preached, respect could turn to rage. He was beaten, chased out of villages and arrested more than once.

From around 1908, Sundar began to travel into Tibet, a mountain land across the Himalayas, where hardly any Christian had ever preached and where outsiders, and especially Christians, were often unwelcome. For years he spent the warmer months crossing the high passes and the winters preaching in India. He also studied for a time at a divinity college in Lahore and was licensed to preach in the Anglican Church, but he gave the licence back so that he could preach freely among Christians of every church, still dressed as a sadhu.

Stories and Questions

Sundar became famous, and with fame came stories. Some of the most remarkable came from his journeys in Tibet: that he had been thrown into a dry well and miraculously rescued by an unseen stranger after three days; that he had met an ancient Christian hermit living high in the mountains; that there was a secret brotherhood of Christian holy men across India. These stories came from Sundar himself, and no one else witnessed them.

In the 1920s, some scholars, including a Jesuit historian in India and a Swiss pastor, examined his accounts and argued that several could not be checked or were not true. Others who investigated defended his honesty. The argument has never been fully settled. Meanwhile, as often happens with famous holy people, other stories about him grew in the retelling, until it can be hard to tell what he said from what was said about him.

It is fair, then, to read the most dramatic Tibetan stories with some caution. What Came After

He had made up his mind: if God did not show himself to him before then, he would go out and lay his head on the rails. He prayed, as he later remembered it, something like this: “O God, if there is a God, wilt thou show me the right way or I will kill myself.” He prayed, and nothing happened. He kept praying. Four o’clock came. Then the minutes went by toward half past four, and the five o’clock train. What happened next, Sundar told for the rest of his life, in India and in Europe and in America, without much change. The room filled with a light. In the light he saw a figure, and he knew who it was. It was Jesus, the one whose book he had burned three days before. Sikh men traditionally leave their hair uncut and wear a turban, and the name Singh, which means “lion,” is shared by Sikh men. His father, Sher Singh, was a landowner, wealthy and well connected. Sundar was the youngest son, and he grew up surrounded by comfort: servants, good food, fine clothes. But his home was open to more than one religious tradition. Holy men of different faiths came and went. Sundar learned the Sikh scriptures, and he also learned the Hindu ones. His biographers were told that by the age of seven he knew much of the Bhagavad Gita, one of the best-loved Hindu holy books, by heart. The great influence of his childhood was his mother. She was deeply devout. She took him to visit sadhus, the wandering holy men of India who give up home, money and comfort to seek God, and she told him that one day he too should seek God like that, and find the peace that only God could give. Years later, when someone suggested that Sundar should go to a theological college, he said he had already been to the best one there was: his mother’s lap. She had been the one who understood his questions. Now she was gone, and the questions remained, sharper than ever. He threw himself into religion with ferocious energy. He read the scriptures of his tradition, and of others. He tried the disciplines of yoga under a Hindu teacher, hoping for the inner stillness it promised. He kept every ceremony. If you feel that way, or have felt it lately, please do not keep it to yourself. Tell an adult you trust today: a parent, a teacher, a youth leader, a school counsellor, a doctor. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number or a crisis line where you live. Sundar was alone with his despair that night, and it nearly killed him. You do not have to be alone with yours. Telling someone is not weakness. It is often the bravest thing a person can do. Sundar told the story of what happened in the early morning many times, and the details stayed remarkably consistent. At about half past four, he said, the room filled with a bright light. At first he thought the house was on fire. Then he saw in the light the figure of a man, and the man’s face had, in Sundar’s words, “such an appearance of glory and love.” He had expected, if anyone appeared, that it might be the Buddha, or Krishna, or one of the holy figures of the traditions he knew.
